articles.title: Teruaki Sato, Cubs Reportedly Agree to Contract, Full Details Revealed in New MLB Rumors
articles.summary: Teruaki Sato is bringing his prodigious power to the Windy City.
articles.body:
Teruaki Sato is bringing his prodigious power to the Windy City.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , Sato and the Chicago Cubs have agreed to terms on an six-year, $120 million contract.

Sato was officially posted by the Hanshin Tigers on Nov. 1, giving MLB teams 45 days to negotiate a deal with his representatives.

As an over-25 player, Sato was not subject to international free-agent rules and could sign for however much a team wanted to pay him. There seemed to be little doubt he would find a home in MLB, especially given the dearth of high-quality hitters in free agency this offseason.

Sato has drawn some comparisons to Munetaka Murakami in ways both good and potentially concerning. The good stems from his big power potential after a combined 79 homers in 283 games over the past two seasons, despite playing in a pitcher-friendly environment that saw teams average 3.4 runs per game in 2026.

On the concerning side, Sato has struck out at least 130 times in each of his five seasons with Hanshin. He also punched out more than 160 times in each of the past two years.

Despite those high totals, The Athletic's Keith Law noted scouts he has talked to about Sato indicate his approach is "better than the raw data would indicate" and he was swinging harder because "that's the expectation given where he's hit in the lineup and since his home park is unfriendly to power."

If Sato ends up making contact at a higher rate and maintain his power, he could be a huge difference-maker for Chicago.

The Cubs had two openings in the outfield with Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ hitting free agency, so it's only natural they would try to take a big swing to fill some of the void.

Chicago had one of the best lineups in MLB last season, led by NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong. They led the league in runs scored, wOBA and wRC+.

It was assumed with an offense that strong and deep, the Cubs would decide to focus most of their attention on the pitching staff.

While it's certainly true the Cubs need to add a couple of arms to their rotation, one way to ease the pressure on the pitching is being able to score runs in bunches.

The addition of Sato puts him in a lineup with Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman, Michael Conforto, Nico Hoerner and Michael Busch.

There are some flaws with the group to nitpick, particularly with how frequently they might strike out, but the upside is enormous for a Cubs team that is chasing the Milwaukee Brewers in the NL Central.

There was already a strong foundation of talent in place for the Cubs to be a playoff contender in 2027. They just needed to add a couple pieces to potentially reach the top level of NL contenders. Sato more than fits the bill as they look to chase down the defending World Series champion Brewers.

articles.title: Teruaki Sato, PCA Headline Updated Cubs Roster, Latest Payroll After Japanese Star's $120M Contract
articles.summary: The Chicago Cubs reportedly added another MVP to their roster on Tuesday.
articles.body:
The Chicago Cubs reportedly added another MVP to their roster on Tuesday.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , the Cubs signed two-time Central League MVP Teruaki Sato to a six-year, $120 million contract, adding him alongside 2026 National League MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong. Chicago entered the day with $155.7 million in total payroll allocations for the 2027 season, which ranked 14th in MLB, per Spotrac .

Chicago has now committed $240 million to two free agents in roughly 12 hours after signing Sato and left-handed pitcher Trevor Rogers to $120 million deals.

Following Sato's signing, the Cubs' lineup now looks like this:

Sato starred for the Hanshin Tigers of Nippon Professional Baseball and won the triple crown this past season, hitting .306 with 39 home runs and 106 RBI in 143 games. The five-time NPB All-Star recorded 40 homers and 102 RBI in 2025. As ESPN's Jesse Rogers noted, the 27-year-old also won a Gold Glove at third base, but the Cubs "are likely to use him in right field, replacing free agent Seiya Suzuki."

"Sato played 45 games in the outfield over the past two years in Japan and is five years younger than Suzuki, making him the more attractive option," Rogers added.

In addition to landing Sato, the Cubs recently signed Rogers, who was described as "one of the best pitchers available." Chicago still has a few holes to fill with the potential departures of pitchers Shota Imanaga, Clay Holmes, Kevin Gausman and David Peterson, but the team is moving in the right direction as it tries to set itself up as a World Series contender.

With Crow-Armstrong and Sato leading the lineup, the Cubs could have the chance to repeat as MLB's No. 1 run-scoring team as they try to compete for a title.

articles.title: Yankees, Mets, Phillies' MLB Top Free-Agent, Trade Targets After Teruaki Sato's Cubs Contract
articles.summary: One of the top hitters in the 2027 MLB free-agent class is now off the board.
articles.body:
One of the top hitters in the 2027 MLB free-agent class is now off the board.

ESPN's Jeff Passan reported Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato agreed to a six-year, $120 million deal with the Chicago Cubs. Sato is the No. 5 overall player in Bleacher Report's free-agent rankings .

The New York Yankees, New York Mets and Philadelphia Phillies were all linked with Sato earlier this month. If strengthening the offense remains a focus, the three will have to pivot to other targets.

Here's who could be on the radar for the trio of contenders.

The Bronx Bombers are heading into 2027 with an infield that could start Ryan McMahon at third and potentially Anthony Volpe at second. McMahon has slugged just .349 since his move to New York, while Volpe has been a below-average hitter since debuting in MLB in 2023.

Alec Bohm or Brandon Lowe would provide an immediate offensive upgrade.

Bohm is coming off a disappointing 2026 season in which he posted a .249/.315/.383 slash line. Hopefully, that's just a one-year blip. Lowe could regress in a different direction after hitting 35 home runs and driving in 96 RBI but is still a proven commodity. His 150 appearances were also a career high.

On the pitching front, the Yankees have pursued Japanese high schooler Shoki Oda. The 18-year-old wouldn't provide immediate help to the starting rotation, but he could be a long-term contributor at a manageable cost if he decides to make the jump to the United States

The Mets might be done big-game hunting after lining up a $450 million deal for two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal.

The Athletic's Will Sammon reported Monday that "some kind of short-term arrangement" is New York's likely route to add any further pitching. The New York Post 's Jon Heyman and Joel Sherman suggested Nick Martinez could be a solution:

Japanese pitcher Kaima Taira, on the other hand, might be a little too pricey for the Mets' tastes. Teams that missed out on Skubal could go after the right-hander even more aggressively.

If New York is willing to keep expanding the payroll, Taira's versatility as a starter and reliever could be worth it.

Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski didn't shy away from laying out his top priority.

"I will say one thing: We have to have an outfielder," he told reporters earlier this month. "Right now, we don't have an outfielder. But is that more important than some other things? I guess it depends upon who that outfielder is."

Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are the best two outfielders available. In the case of the latter, Sato's agreement with Chicago could mean a reunion to the Cubs is off the table.

Especially if the bidding climbs into the nine figures, Philly would be right to have some reservations about signing either player. But the fans will voice their frustration if the team fails to bring serious reinforcements to the outfield.

articles.title: Freddy Peralta, Orioles Reportedly Agree to Contract amid Latest MLB Free Agency Rumors
articles.summary: After being traded twice in 2026, ace pitcher Freddy Peralta is once again joining a new team ahead of the 2027 season.
articles.body:
After being traded twice in 2026, ace pitcher Freddy Peralta is once again joining a new team ahead of the 2027 season.

According to The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal , Peralta and the Baltimore Orioles agreed to terms on a five-year, $125 million deal that includes no opt-outs or deferrals.

The two-time All-Star ended the 2026 campaign with the Tampa Bay Rays after the team acquired him at the Aug. 2 trade deadline from the New York Mets, who had previously acquired him from the Milwaukee Brewers last January.

Peralta became one of the most coveted pitchers on the trade market after his stellar 2025 season with the Brewers, going 17-6 with a career-best 2.70 ERA and 204 strikeouts. However, his tenure with the Mets didn't go that well.

In 22 starts in New York, Peralta went 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA and a 1.48 WHIP. The Mets endured a disappointing season that culminated in a last-place finish in the NL East, so they sold assets at the trade deadline, sending Peralta to the Rays.

After joining one of this year's top World Series contenders, Peralta quickly got his groove back. He went 4-0 in September with a 0.96 ERA, earning AL Pitcher of the Month honors. In 10 regular-season starts for Tampa Bay, he went 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA and a 1.01 WHIP. He appeared in five playoff games with four starts, going 2-1 with a 2.95 ERA as the Rays lost to the Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series in five games.

Now, Peralta will be taking his talents to an Orioles squad that went 79-82 in 2026 and missed the playoffs for the second straight year. He should immediately take over as the team's ace as Baltimore chases a playoff spot next year.

articles.title: Chicago Cubs begin rotation rebuild with signing of Trevor Rogers
articles.summary: Acquiring the former Oriole is a big first step for a Cubs team in dire need of pitching reinforcements.
articles.body:
This award season was a fruitful one for the 2026 Chicago Cubs.

Besides Pete Crow-Armstrong's individual NL MVP honors, the club took home the team awards for both the Gold Glove and Silver Slugger. It marked the first time in the history of those categories that the same team was crowned for both its defensive and offensive prowess.

You'd think a team with such accomplishments could win a playoff game.

Alas, a combination of baseball randomness and underwhelming pitching sent the Cubs packing in a swift wild-card round drubbing by the San Diego Padres. Chicago president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer can do little to combat baseball randomness. But the pitching is a different story, especially because so much of Chicago's 2026 staff is no longer with the club.

Ten pitchers started at least three games for the 2026 Cubs. Just two of those, Edward Cabrera and Javier Assad, project to factor into the plans for all of 2027. Full-season fixtures Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd and Colin Rea all reached free agency. So too did midseason pick-ups David Peterson, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes. Jameson Taillon was dealt at the trade deadline. Ben Brown remains in the organization but underwent spine surgery in early November and likely won't be a full-go until the middle of next year.

It's worth noting that Justin Steele (2023 Cy Young fifth-place finisher) and Cade Horton (2025 NL Rookie of the Year runner-up) are both set to return from the injuries that kept them sidelined for all and most of 2026, respectively. But while their impending reemergences should help bolster Chicago's staff, it's difficult to imagine both of them recapturing their best right away.

And so, this was a group in dire need of external reinforcements. How Hoyer would go about rebuilding Chicago's rotation was one of the most fascinating storylines entering this MLB offseason.

Late Monday night, the Cubs took a massive step forward in patching their pitching hole by reportedly agreeing to terms with southpaw Trevor Rogers on a five-year, $120 million contract . Rogers, who turned 29 years old this month, was considered the second-best left-handed starter of this free-agent class , behind the incomparable Tarik Skubal. The yet-to-be-confirmed deal features incentive escalators as well as deferrals that will lessen the true value.

Even still, it's a hefty chunk of change for a pitcher who has surpassed 133 innings in a season just once in his career. Drafted as a first-round pick by the Miami Marlins in 2017, Rogers announced himself in 2021 with a dynamite Rookie of the Year runner-up campaign in which he posted a 2.64 ERA across 25 starts. Then the wheels fell off. Over the next three injury-marred seasons, the Carlsbad, New Mexico, kid delivered an ugly 5.09 ERA in nearly 250 innings. Miami sent him to Baltimore at the 2024 deadline. Baltimore promptly sent him to Triple-A after four horrid starts.

But in 2025, Rogers reemerged as a force, thanks in large part to an offseason stint at the Driveline training facility in Arizona that helped him rediscover some fastball velocity. After a kneecap dislocation delayed the start to his season, he pitched to a microscopic 1.81 ERA across 18 starts, earning down-ballot Cy Young votes. His 2026 season was a bit more uneven (4.03 in 169 2/3), but the underlying metrics were kinder, and Rogers' ability to take the ball 30 times bolstered his status as a frontline guy.

For the Cubs, Rogers is an intriguing, if somewhat risky choice to helm the rotation. He has never started a postseason game and has yet to prove himself capable of shouldering a full workload in back-to-back seasons. Steele and/or Horton should slot in alongside Rogers once they return, and the Cubs are surely counting on a bounce-back season from Edward Cabrera as well.

Are the Cubs better today than they were when their season ended? It's tough to say. The reported addition of Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato will help cover the potential departures of Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ. Rogers makes the rotation better, surely, but Hoyer still needs to add another arm or two to really shore up the group.

articles.title: Cubs make another big splash, add more power to their lineup with Teruaki Sato
articles.summary: The Japanese slugger was arguably the best hitter on this year's free-agent market.
articles.body:
With the expiration of the collective bargaining agreement rapidly approaching on Dec. 1, the Chicago Cubs clearly decided they were not going to be shut out in this first round of MLB free agency. Just hours after landing left-hander Trevor Rogers on a five-year, $120 million deal, the Cubs made another huge splash Tuesday, agreeing with Japanese star Teruaki Sato on a six-year, $120 million deal .

Sato, 27, was arguably the best hitter on this year's free-agent market . The-two time NPB Central League MVP has been a terror for pitchers, batting .306 with 39 home runs and 106 RBI in 143 games last season for the Hanshin Tigers en route to winning the Triple Crown and his second consecutive MVP award.

Power is Sato's calling card. The Japanese slugger has launched 167 homers over six seasons in NPB, including 40 home runs in 2025 and 39 last season.

The downside to the five-time NPB All-Star's game is the significant swing-and-miss, as he averaged 163 strikeouts the past two seasons. While the contact concerns with Sato aren't quite as great as they were with countryman and White Sox first baseman Munetaka Murakami, it is a part of his game.

This is a critical offseason for the Cubs, who went into the winter needing not only starting pitching reinforcements but also outfield help. Both the team's corner outfielders, Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki, are currently free agents, and it always seemed unlikely that both would return. Sato's arrival appears to confirm that, given that while he played third base in Japan, he's considered a better fit in the outfield in MLB.

The Cubs' offense was their biggest strength in 2026. Led by National League MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong, the team led baseball in runs scored. Sato will further reinforce the lineup and also have plenty of protection, likely sandwiched between Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman.

Chicago president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer was quiet through the beginning of this offseason, but in a span of 12 hours, his team landed two of the best free agents on the market in Sato ( No. 6 on Yahoo's list ) and Rogers (No. 8). After watching the Milwaukee Brewers hoist their first World Series title in 2026, it was difficult to imagine that the rivals 90 minutes south were going to sit idly this winter.

Instead, this is now back-to-back offseasons with the Chicago Cubs taking big swings in free agency. Last winter, the Cubs landed Bregman to anchor the middle of their lineup, and that move was a huge success in the third baseman's first season in Chicago.

The Cubs remaining work to be done this winter is in their rotation and bullpen. Even after the signing of Rogers, Chicago has a few spots in the rotation to fill and a relief corps to reinforce.

articles.title: MLBPA Responds to MLB's Latest Salary Cap Proposal in CBA Talks with Lockout Looming
articles.summary: The MLB Players Association remains unsatisfied with MLB's latest adjustment to its salary cap proposal ahead of the looming Dec. 1 deadline to ratify a new collective bargaining agreement.
articles.body:
The MLB Players Association remains unsatisfied with MLB's latest adjustment to its salary cap proposal ahead of the looming Dec. 1 deadline to ratify a new collective bargaining agreement.

MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer objected in a statement, shared by The Athletic's Evan Drellich , to MLB's withdrawal of escrow from its proposed salary cap on Tuesday.

MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said in a statement no player compensation would be held in escrow under the new CBA proposal, "removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed."

Meyer said in his response the modification provided "no real benefit" to players under the proposed salary cap and floor system.

"Instead of holding back player money each year, MLB's new proposal is to take that same amount of money out of players' pockets in the following year," Meyer wrote.

"It's a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap — to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement. This is yet another example of how MLB's salary cap proposal pits player against player, past, present, and future."

MLB's proposed change states that "any aggregate underpayment or overpayment to players in a given season will be incorporated into the calculation of the salary cap and floor in future seasons."

ESPN's Jeff Passan reported in July the MLBPA was "skeptical of an escrow system that would withhold hundreds of millions more in salaries because caps are based on estimates."

Passan noted that if MLB revenue is less than estimated "some of that withheld money could remain in the teams' hands, essentially making their agreed-upon contracts not fully guaranteed like they are today."

The NBA uses a salary cap system with escrow, through which 10 percent of player salaries are withheld until the league can guarantee revenue is correctly distributed into a 51-49 split between players and owners after the season, per Sportico's Kurt Badenhausen .

When the league's revenue came short of targets in 2025, players forfeited more than $480 million from the escrow fund, Badenhausen reported.

Players in the NHL (50-50 revenue split) lost at least 10 percent of their paychecks to escrow for six straight seasons ahead of the COVID-19 pandemic, per Sportico , but the league stopped taking money for escrow in January 2025.

NHL players received a record $170 million rebate through escrow after the league exceeded revenue targets in 2025-26, per Badenhausen .

It sounds like promising MLB players money won't be taken out of their initial paychecks in pursuit of a 50-50 revenue split hasn't swayed the MLBPA when the money could still be docked from their pay in future seasons.

This isn't the first time MLB has attempted to sway MLBPA toward accepting a cap-and-floor system by making modifications to its offer. MLB updated its pitch Monday to include increases in minimum salary as well as salary arbitration bonuses and veteran player signing bonuses, per MLB.com's Anthony Castrovince .

Meyer responded to the proposal (h/t Drellich ) by saying MLB hadn't added "a single dollar in overall player compensation," and that "any supposed benefits to certain classes of players are simply taken out of the pockets of other players and are vastly outweighed by the negative effects of the cap and MLB's other restrictions."

The current CBA is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET next Tuesday. If no new deal is in place by that time, MLB teams will no longer be able to make transactions or communicate with players, per ESPN's Alden Gonzalez .

articles.title: Japanese Pitcher Kaima Taira, Blue Jays Reportedly Agree to Contract in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Having missed out on Tarik Skubal, the Toronto Blue Jays at least managed to snag one of the best pitchers still available.
articles.body:
Having missed out on Tarik Skubal, the Toronto Blue Jays at least managed to snag one of the best pitchers still available.

The New York Post 's Jon Heyman reported the team agreed to a five-year, $80 million contract with Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira. Taira will have the opportunity to opt out after the third year.

The Athletic's Mitch Bannon reported Toronto was "looking mainly for a pitcher who can impact postseason games." Given his skill set, the playoffs are where Taira might shine in MLB.

The 27-year-old was used primarily as a reliever in 2025. He posted a 1.71 ERA and struck out 53 batters in 52.2 innings, finishing with 31 saves.

This past season, Taira returned to a starting role and was equally effective. His ERA actually dropped to 1.36, and his strikeout rate remained nearly the same. He fanned 141 batters in 146 innings.

Taira carries plenty of risk. There's no telling how he'll fare with the transition to MLB, and he's undersized for the position at 5'8".

Still, he throws eight different pitches and boasts a fastball that sits in the mid-90s. It's not hard to see why the Blue Jays and others were after him.

For now, Taira will probably settle into the back half of Toronto's rotation. If he struggles, a move into the bullpen could be in store, and that might be where he settles regardless in a postseason setting. He could theoretically be a high-leverage option capable of going multiple innings.

Skubal got a record-setting $450 million from the New York Mets. ESPN's Jeff Passan reported Trevor Rogers and Freddy Peralta will earn $120 million and $125 million , respectively, on five-year contracts.

There's a chance Taira is pound-for-pound one of the best pitching signings from this offseason.

articles.title: Winners and Losers of Teruaki Sato, Cubs Agreeing to $120M Contract in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Chicago Cubs fans went to sleep Monday night with news that the team had signed Trevor Rogers in free agency, then woke up Tuesday to another marquee addition: Teruaki Sato.
articles.body:
Chicago Cubs fans went to sleep Monday night with news that the team had signed Trevor Rogers in free agency, then woke up Tuesday to another marquee addition: Teruaki Sato.

The reigning NPB Triple Crown winner and two-time Central League MVP hit .306/.383/.609 with 40 doubles, 39 home runs and 106 RBI last season for the Hanshin Tigers, and he joins the Cubs on a six-year, $120 million deal.

His departure helps offset the loss of his World Baseball Classic teammate Seiya Suzuki, who will almost certainly sign elsewhere in free agency, and that is not the only ripple effect this transaction has on the league.

Ahead, we've highlighted the most notable winners and losers of the Sato signing, providing some broader context to what the move means for the rest of the baseball world.

Loser: Teams Looking for Left-Handed Power

With Jake Bauers agreeing to a four-year, $58 million deal with the Red Sox earlier this month and Sato now off the market, the well has quickly run dry for teams looking to add some left-handed thump to the middle of their lineups.

Second baseman Brandon Lowe remains a top-tier option, coming off a 2026 season in which he posted a 121 OPS+ and hit 35 home runs to win NL Silver Slugger honors.

After him, the drop-off is steep, with veterans Joc Pederson, Josh Bell, Trent Grisham and Ian Happ among the lefty swing or switch-hitting options with some track record of power production.

The X-factor in this corner of the market is Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is just a year removed from a 31-homer season, though his production crashed back to earth in his contract year and he's likely looking at a short-term deal to rebuild value.

Winner: Toronto's Pursuit of Seiya Suzuki

The Toronto Blue Jays have been linked to a variety of high-profile free agents, including Tarik Skubal, Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers, and they got in on the pitching fun on Tuesday when they signed Kaima Taira to a five-year, $80 million deal.

The Sato signing might now steer their potential No. 1 target toward Toronto.

"This offseason, said a league source who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss offseason plans, the Jays are expected to pursue Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki," wrote Mitch Bannon of The Athletic.

That might sound like any other offseason rumbling linking player and team, but this came all the way back on Sept. 28, before the regular season even ended.

With a reunion on the North Side now unlikely and the Blue Jays ready to spend, Suzuki might be one of the next major dominoes to fall, and Toronto looks like the clear favorite to sign him.

Loser: The Yankees' Financial Limitations

Immediately after the Sato signing, Brendan Kuty of The Athletic said the Yankees were never considered serious contenders to sign the Japanese star, despite their glaring need for an upgrade at his natural position at third base.

He was expected to fall outside the team's budget.

With an estimated luxury tax payroll nearing $300 million, they already face one of baseball's most expensive rosters. Add the uncertainty around the CBA negotiations, and their hesitation to spend big is understandable.

Still, at a time when other major market teams are throwing caution to the wind, "outside the team's budget" is likely not a phrase any Yankees fan wants to hear.

In the short term, Teruaki Sato's move stateside will open up the Central League MVP race after he won in 2025 and is a lock for 2026. Sato would have been the clear front-runner again.

Zooming out, the market is robust for the next wave of NPB stars to descend on Major League Baseball and land a massive payday.

Last winter, Munetaka Murakami, Kazuma Okamoto and Tatsuya Imai represented three high-profile players making the MLB jump, but their earning power proved largely unpredictable.

The performances of Murakami and Okamoto, both of whom hit 30 home runs in their MLB debuts, have helped ease concerns about whether a swing-and-miss slugger's power translates from NPB to MLB.

The groundwork has been laid for Shugo Maki, Shota Morishita and others to cash in when their opportunity comes.

Loser: The Brewers' NL Central Stranglehold

With a young, cost-controlled core in place and a dominant postseason run to the franchise's first World Series title still visible in the rearview mirror, the Milwaukee Brewers are well positioned for sustainable success.

In the words of the great Lee Corso: "Not so fast, my friend!"

The Cubs have the reigning NL MVP in Pete Crow-Armstrong, the league's most potent offense from 2026, landed a new staff ace in Trevor Rogers and now added Sato's power bat to the mix.

With more money to spend as they retool the rotation, the Cubs are poised to be a serious threat to the Brewers for NL Central supremacy and, at the very least, have put themselves in a position to be a serious roadblock to their pursuit of a fifth straight NL Central title.

Winner: Munetaka Murakami's Earning Power

MLB Trade Rumors predicted an eight-year, $180 million contract for Munetaka Murakami in their free-agency predictions article last offseason, and some believed early on that his contract could exceed $200 million.

He ended up signing a two-year, $34 million deal with the Chicago White Sox, as concerns that his elevated strikeout rate would become untenable stateside drove down his market.

While he racked up 196 strikeouts in 127 games, he still had enough offensive meat to post a 130 OPS+ with 35 home runs and 2.2 WAR at the center of the South Siders' rise to contention.

Many of those same swing-and-miss concerns are present in Sato's profile, but, no doubt due in part to Murakami's success in 2026, he secured the nine-figure payday.

Next offseason, when he hits the open market again, Murakami should be much better positioned reel in that $100 million payday given Sato's contract as a still unproven MLB performer.

With an aging core of high-priced stars, the Philadelphia Phillies looked like the perfect team to make a run at signing Sato, who, at 27, is several years younger than the other top bats on the market.

The Phillies also clearly need another run producer with Alec Bohm departing in free agency, and they have a glaring hole to fill at one of the corner outfield spots alongside Brandon Marsh and Justin Crawford.

He was never explicitly named the team's top target, but Sato was likely No. 1 on Philadelphia's offseason big board.

Now, the pivot will likely be a push to sign Randy Arozarena (31) or Seiya Suzuki (32) to address the need for another power bat by targeting a corner outfielder, and that will add another expensive player on the wrong side of 30 to the payroll, provided they don't come up short in that pursuit as well.

The Phillies still have plenty of talent, but their window is closing, and whiffing on Sato feels like another nudge toward it slamming shut.

The Cubs made a splash on Monday night when they inked Trevor Rogers to a five-year, $120 million deal and carried that momentum into the morning with the Sato signing.

They essentially swapped out Ian Happ and Shota Imanaga for the two newcomers without adding more than a few million dollars to the books.

Beyond that, Chicago seems like the perfect fit for Sato's stateside debut.

The organization has a well-established NPB-to-MLB pipeline, which should help make the transition smoother. Playing alongside an elite defensive center fielder like Pete Crow-Armstrong will also ease the pressure of transitioning to full-time outfield.

Beyond their clear need for pitching help, the biggest potential blow to the Cubs' 2027 outlook was losing Seiya Suzuki and failing to replace his middle-of-the-order presence. The Cubs did that on Tuesday and got four years younger in the process.

There will be growing pains, and the swing-and-miss concerns are not unfounded, but the Cubs have a well-rounded enough offensive attack to offset a strikeout-heavy profile if the trade-off is 30 home runs.

A terrific 24 hours for the Cubs, no question, and now they will look to put the finishing touches on the pitching staff.

articles.title: MLB free agency Top 50: Ranking the best players available this winter, with Tarik Skubal and Freddy Peralta off the board
articles.summary: This free-agent class is notably light on top-tier talent, particularly when it comes to position players.
articles.body:
Buckle up, friends. A very odd free-agent season is here.

With the sport hurtling toward an elongated work stoppage and labor battle, this offseason projects to be disjointed, chaotic and boring all at the same time. When the existing collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, MLB will lurch into a transactional dead period. As team owners and the MLBPA bargain over the game's future , general managers, agents and players will, for the most part, be twiddling their thumbs and waiting around. That oncoming storm should precipitate a flurry of moves in the days and hours leading up to that Dec. 1 deadline, which is how things went five years ago during the 2021-22 lockout.

This free-agent class, however, is notably light on top-tier talent. That's particularly true on the position-player side, where, for the first time in a decade, no hitter is expected to receive a nine-figure contract. Still, there are a bevy of corner outfielders and more every-day second basemen than we can ever remember seeing on the open market. There's also a lot of starting pitching; 12 hurlers who started a postseason game in 2026 are set to become free agents, with top arm and first major domino Tarik Skubal having already signed with the Mets .

The lack of impact bats could spark a friskier than normal trade market, though the lockout will probably stunt that to a degree. Nobody really knows how the labor showdown is going to play out. Opening Day could happen on schedule. We could miss months of the 2027 season. It's a total mystery.

If you're looking for certainty, please direct your attention to the following list of free agents, ranked meticulously in the inarguably correct order.

Note: An asterisk indicates a player received a qualifying offer of one year, $23.15 million from his former team. Ages listed are for the 2027 season (age on June 30, 2027). You can find a full list of pending free agents here .

A man in his own tier. No matter how you slice it, no matter whom you ask, the two-time Cy Young winner is the premier prize of this class, and it's not particularly close. And the Mets treated him accordingly.

Skubal entered the season on track to challenge for the single largest free-agent contract ever handed out to a pitcher, a record held by Yoshinobu Yamamoto at $325 million. But in early May, things got squirrely in a hurry when the then-Tigers southpaw missed a start due to elbow discomfort. Thankfully, scans revealed no ligament damage. Instead, Skubal underwent an innovative, new procedure to remove bone chips in his elbow. He was back on a big-league mound by June 13. It was a remarkably quick comeback.

As the Tigers continued to wallow on the outer fringes of the AL wild-card race, attention turned toward Skubal as a trade chip. Just a few days before the deadline, the two-time defending champion Dodgers pounced, sending a trio of prospects to Detroit for the all-world southpaw and sending much of the baseball world into yet another round of anti-Dodgers agita.

In L.A., Skubal blocked out the noise and kept on carving, working to a 2.61 ERA across 10 regular-season starts. He threw twice during the club's abbreviated October run, in 100-degree heat against the Braves in NLDS Game 1 and against the NL champion Brewers in NLCS Game 1 . Both of those outings were shorter than he or the Dodgers would've liked, but for the most part, Skubal looked like Skubal.

So while 2026 wasn't the smooth, problem-free walk year that Skubal might've hoped for, he ultimately conquered free agency with a record-breaking deal. Given the uncertainty surrounding the impending lockout and the new financial landscape that might emerge, Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras, moved quickly to secure a deal before the baseball world goes dark on Dec. 1.

This October, "Fastball Freddy" looked completely rejuvenated with the Rays after a bizarrely bad, abbreviated stint with the Mets. His velocity climbed back up to career-best levels, and his nasty changeup played up as a result, making him nearly untouchable down the stretch and into the postseason, where his remarkable trajectory was reviewed on national broadcasts as he pitched his way to ALCS MVP honors .

When Peralta arrived at Mets spring training in February, there was little questioning his status as the second-best free-agent-pitcher-to-be after Skubal. The question by the end of the season was how much damage did he do to his stock while wearing blue and orange? Based on his larger track record, those few months sure look like an untimely outlier. And given that he looked as good as ever as a Ray, the Orioles were comfortable giving him the nine-figure deal that seemed to be slipping away in the season's first half. Given Peralta's October performance, Baltimore can feel confident that they are adding an impact pitcher capable of being a difference-maker when the stakes are highest.

Suzuki made good on the five-year, $85 million deal he signed with the Cubs when he came stateside after starring in Japan's NPB, and now he hits the open market again with a chance to exceed that first MLB contract as arguably the top free-agent hitter. While Suzuki's relative youth enhanced his earning power five years ago, he now has a half-decade of proven big-league production that should enamor teams seeking an impact bat.

The 2026 season featured a few interesting developments in Suzuki's profile: a big step forward with his outfield defense and a notable decline in his underlying batted-ball metrics (career-low hard-hit and barrel rates), while his surface-level stats (26 HR, .841 OPS) remained quite strong and he walked at a career-high 12.4% clip. That Suzuki seems to have restored his stock as an every-day right fielder, rather than one trending toward DH-only, is a pretty big deal and part of why he gets a slight edge in our rankings over a similar bat but worse defender in Randy Arozarena. The subtle declines in Suzuki's offensive game are worth considering as he enters his mid-30s, but this is still a terrific right-handed slugger who would upgrade any lineup. Expect him to get paid accordingly after declining the qualifying offer.

Since bursting on the scene with a legendary hot streak with the Rays in the 2020 postseason, Arozarena has been one of the most reliably entertaining and productive position players in MLB. He was one of the few bright spots amid an otherwise disastrous Mariners campaign in 2026, delivering his best regular season at the best possible time and setting career highs in batting average (.281), on-base percentage (.381), slugging percentage (.484) and fWAR (5.5). As always, Arozarena racked up some gaudy counting stats along the way: He joined Barry Bonds, Bobby Bonds, Bobby Abreu and Willie Mays as the fifth player ever to record six consecutive seasons with 20-plus homers and 20-plus stolen bases.

That's the kind of stunning fun fact that Boras, Arozarena's agent, is likely to seize on as he tries to sell teams on the outfielder as the best bat in this free-agent class. However, Arozarena, who declined the Mariners' qualifying offer, is not without his flaws, and his longstanding reputation as a poor (and sometimes lackadaisical) glove at a position already far down the defensive spectrum (left field) is going to scare off some teams forecast a downtick in offensive output coming sooner rather than later; after all, his underlying metrics don't jump out as much as his surface-level stats. Still, in this shallow class, it would hardly be surprising if Boras can convince a club to splurge on a player with Arozarena's steady track record and unique star power.

King's decision to opt out and test the open market probably says more about the market than it does the $58 million he's forgoing. However, the affable righty was incredibly effective in 2026, reaching 185 innings for the first time in his career with a crisp 3.21 ERA. The peripherals were a bit less friendly, but this is definitely a guy you can feel comfortable starting in Game 1 of a playoff series. King's willingness to work out of the bullpen in the NLDS only added to his reputation.

Relying on a sinker-changeup combo means King is also relatively platoon-neutral; in fact, he was actually better against lefties than righties this season. That mix, the athleticism, the playoff pedigree, the improved durability; it all comes together to make an enticing package. King is squarely the third-best starter available.

The clear headliner among this offseason's wave of players making the jump from Japan's NPB is Sato, a left-handed slugger with titanic raw power who has taken his game to new heights over the past couple of years. A solid power bat with the Hanshin Tigers earlier in his career, Sato's stock exploded in 2025, when he hit .277/.345 .579 with 40 homers in 139 games. That made him look like Babe Ruth during the dead-ball era, as Sato's stupendous slugging stood out at a time when offense in NPB has been notably down; just one other hitter hit more than 23 home runs in 2025 (Franmil Reyes with 32). Sato's breakout raised expectations for 2026, and somehow he exceeded them, slashing .306/.383/.609 with 39 homers in 143 games.

Stylistically, it's tempting to compare Sato to last winter's prodigious Japanese lefty slugger, Munetaka Murakami. Murakami's profile was fiercely debated until the White Sox signed him to a smaller deal than expected, and he proceeded to have a largely successful but predictably volatile rookie campaign. From a raw power standpoint, Sato and Murakami are roughly on the same level, with Murakami having the slight edge, though both are capable of punishing balls with exit velocities in excess of 115 mph. Sato's strikeout rate has hovered around 27% the past two seasons, while Murakami's was closer to 30%.

The crucial distinction between the two players' plate discipline profiles is that while Sato whiffs less (especially in-zone) than Murakami, he chases significantly more pitches outside the strike zone. So while Sato might not strike out as often as Murakami, he might have a much tougher time offsetting those strikeouts with walks. The other element tilting in Sato's favor is his defensive outlook. He is not a definitive lock to stay at third base, but he has the athleticism to warrant a longer look at the hot corner than Murakami, who was immediately moved to first. Sato and his strong arm could also profile well in a corner outfield spot. Of course, it's still all about the bat, for which he got paid handsomely.

The long-time Padre, who declined the team's qualifying offer, is one of the more compelling characters available this winter. He ranked third in 2026 in innings pitched by relievers (86), which lends credence to a team being interested in stretching Morejón out into a starter. A sturdy four-pitch mix (sinker, changeup, slider, four-seam) is another indicator that the stout Cuban could make the leap to a rotation. And even if nobody bites on that transition, Morejón is still the most enticing bullpen arm on the market. He is one of just four relievers with more than 60 innings pitched and an ERA under 3.00 in each of the past three seasons (Mason Miller, Tyler Rogers, Cade Smith). Layer on his age — Morejón doesn't turn 28 until February — and you've got the makings of a four-year deal.

Very few pitchers over the past few seasons have oscillated between dominance and disaster as frequently and as drastically as the former Oriole. Rogers came to Baltimore at the 2024 trade deadline and was downright unviable for the remainder of that season, earning him a demotion to Triple-A. Then he reappeared in the Show mid-May 2025 and put together 18 magnificent starts, earning him down-ballot Cy Young votes. The 2026 season was Jekyll mixed with Hyde. Rogers had a seven-start stretch with a 10.01 ERA and a seven-start stretch with a 1.69 ERA. His final season numbers were a reflection of that inconsistency, though a 3.45 FIP points toward brighter days.

So why is Rogers, who declined the Orioles' qualifying offer, ranked this high? Pitchers rarely hit the open market this young, coming off a 160-plus-inning season and having, at some point, showcased this level of impact. The Cubs clearly saw a frontline starter lurking beneath the surface here and paid Rogers accordingly.

Milwaukee's former cleanup hitter is more than just a sensational October hero story ; Bauers raked all season. And somehow, the underlying metrics are even more bullish. Only two qualified hitters this season finished in the top 10th percentile in hard-hit rate, launch-angle sweet spot rate and barrel percentage: Bauers and unanimous AL MVP Yordan Alvarez . Impressively, Bauers also ran a higher walk rate than Alvarez, though he struck out significantly more.

There are holes in his game, to be sure. Besides the strikeouts, Bauers is a poor defensive first baseman who can fake it in the outfield but probably shouldn't. There's also such a small track record of production at this level. Still, given the dearth of difference-making bats on the market, Bauers got a real payday from the Red Sox.

Jeffers was enjoying a career year when a left hamate fracture in May sidelined him for two months, an untimely sequence, as he never quite restored his top-tier form down the stretch before reaching free agency. Still, there's a lot to like about Jeffers' game. Catchers with his combo of contact skills and solid power are rare; his 119 wRC+ over the past four seasons ranks eighth among his qualified positional peers . The glovework is OK at best, but it's sufficient for the Twins to want to keep him around.

Lowe's one season in Pittsburgh — he was traded there from Tampa Bay last winter — was probably the most productive and complete of his career. The nine-year vet appeared in a career-best 150 games, clobbered 35 long balls and turned himself into a legitimately great second-base defender. Health has always been the biggest bugaboo for the former Maryland Terrapin, but whenever he plays more than 110 games, he reaches the 30-homer mark. Not a bad schtick in our opinion. There's enough here, particularly with the defensive breakout, to think a team would commit to Lowe, who declined the Pirates' qualifying offer, for three seasons.

Before the 2026 season, Chisholm boldly proclaimed that he intended to clock 50 homers and steal 50 bags, something accomplished only by Shohei Ohtani in 2024. Instead, Chisholm delivered a womp-womp of a walk year, finishing the campaign with a roughly league-average batting line, 19 homers and 41 steals. That's a productive player but not the franchise-altering force many thought Chisholm could become. It was also a big step back from his encouraging 2025, in which Chisholm went 30/30, posted an OPS over .800, made the All-Star team and won a Silver Slugger Award.

One can spend ample time dissecting what Chisholm isn't, but it's also worth pointing out what he is. The gregarious Bahamian is one of the most valuable baserunners in the sport, a speedster with great feel for life on the bases. His glove, too, grades out phenomenally well at the keystone. That creates a really high floor, one that might convince teams to take a risk on the other, more mercurial pieces of the puzzle. If it ever fully clicks, Chisholm could compete for an MVP. If he can replicate his 2025, he's an immensely valuable player. But is anybody willing to pay to find out?

Pitchers this old rarely get multi-year deals. Gray's one season in Boston was a smashing success, even if the peripherals were a tad more pessimistic than the surface-level stats. The durability (age aside) is also a calling card; Gray is one of just nine starters who have surpassed 160 innings in each of the past three seasons (Tanner Bibee, Dylan Cease, Kevin Gausman, Freddy Peralta, Cristopher Sánchez, Framber Valdez, Michael Wacha, Logan Webb). Veteran playoff starters don't grow on trees.

Speaking of veteran playoff starters, Mahle cemented his resurgent second half in Atlanta with two stellar postseason outings. Traded from the Giants to the Braves at the deadline, he was even more valuable on a run-prevention basis than Tarik Skubal. Atlanta upped the usage on his split-finger, which led to a nice bump in chase rate and ground-ball rate. Mahle then surrendered just two earned runs across 13 1/3 playoff innings against two very dangerous lineups (Philly and Los Angeles). Admittedly, it's a small, recent sample of effectiveness. But that's enough nowadays. It felt like Mahle was earning himself another million with each postseason punchout. We think he gets three years.

We think Adrian Morejón will get paid like a converted starter, which is why Bednar got our "best reliever available" label. The Pittsburgh-raised closer ranks fifth in saves since the start of 2025, with 62, and is one of just six relievers with 60 innings pitched and an ERA under 3.00 in each of the past two seasons (Miller, Morejón, Rogers, Smith, Louis Varland). Given all the buzz and weight and noise, being The Closer for the New York Yankees does indeed carry an added level of pressure, pressure that Bednar handled with aplomb. He has an even-keeled comportment and a dialed three-pitch mix (even split of splitters and four-seamers with some curveballs scattered in).

For nearly a half-decade, Happ was the paragon of consistency, one of just eight players to appear in at least 150 games and post an OPS+ above 115 every season from 2022 to 2025 (Pete Alonso, Vlad Guerrero Jr., Francisco Lindor, Matt Olson, José Ramírez, Kyle Schwarber and Juan Soto). But the 10-year Cubbie endured a relative down year at a bummer of a time, with career lows in a swath of important categories in 2026. Still, there are myriad reasons to believe in Happ's profile moving forward. The switch-hitter still walks a ton, rarely chases, plays great outfield defense and knocks the ball into the seats. A reunion with either Happ or Suzuki feels like a reasonable course of action for the Cubs, but this is one of the free-agent situations where the impending lockout could make things complicated.

Arraez spent most of 2026 debunking the league-wide doubts that lingered over his free agency last winter before he landed with the Giants on a one-year, $12 million deal. He made his fourth career All-Star Game, dramatically improved as a defender at second base and spent most of the year battling for a batting title. But his performance post-trade with Philadelphia wasn't great, and an ankle injury in September rendered him unavailable for the Phillies' brief postseason run. That sends Arraez back into free agency on a less inspiring note than he seemed to be trending toward. His lack of power remains an inescapable limiting factor for teams considering giving Arraez a multiyear deal, but his transformation with the glove should strengthen his market relative to what he experienced last year.

After accepting the qualifying offer from Detroit last winter, Torres made two trips to the injured list during the 2026 season due to a left oblique strain, which resulted in his fewest games ever played (96) in a full major-league season. But while the sample (420 plate appearances) was smaller due to the missed time, Torres' .364 OBP in 2026 was a career high. Less encouraging was a career-low .363 slugging percentage. He's a negative on defense and on the basepaths, but Torres' advanced on-base skills should appeal to teams trying to lengthen their lineups. A healthier version of Torres probably slugs a bit more, too.

Simply put, big-league pitchers are not built like Taira. At 5-foot-8 and roughly 220 pounds, Taira's only physical comparison on a major-league pitching staff is late-blooming Baltimore bullpen arm Rico Garcia (5-foot-9, 215 lbs.). That complete lack of parallels — along with the fact that Taira has spent only two of his nine seasons with the Seibu Lions in the rotation (2023 and 2026) — is why there is skepticism that Taira can hold up as a starter stateside. In 2026, there were only three full-time starters (Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Shota Imanaga, Sonny Gray) listed at 5-foot-10, and only three more pitchers of any role were listed shorter than that (Garcia and Sam Moll at 5-foot-9, plus Yuki Matsui at 5-foot-8).

We probably should've mentioned already that Taira's career ERA in 592 NPB innings is 1.78, including a league-best 1.36 across 146 frames in 2026 as he transitioned back to the rotation in anticipation of making the jump to MLB this offseason. His return to a starting role allowed him to showcase his diverse repertoire beyond his headlining heater that averages 96 mph; he also attacked with an 83-mph slider (20%), a 91-mph cutter (18%), an 88-mph changeup (11%) and an 85-mph splitter (9%). At the very least, Taira's having thrived as a reliever earlier in his career gives him and the Blue Jays a fallback plan if his quest to stick in the rotation doesn't go well. Taira is a special talent — and quite young for a free-agent pitcher — so his transition to the majors will be monitored with great curiosity.

Holmes' transition from All-Star reliever to rock-solid rotation option has been impressive. Is there another gear for him to reach as a starter, even in his mid-30s, or is the cement dry on his profile as an extreme groundball artist with minimal whiff potential and a sturdy floor as a regular-season innings-eater? At the very least, whichever team scoops up Holmes will want to have a stellar infield defense behind him.

The former No. 1 overall draft pick looked to finally be living up to his draft status with a terrific first half (2.79 ERA in 77 ⅓ innings) that earned him his first All-Star invite. But the right-hander was downright dismal (7.46 ERA in 44 ⅔ innings) after being traded to San Diego and finished the season on the injured list due to an ankle sprain. His limited track record of top-notch run prevention and his troubling injury history might scare off some clubs, but it's not hard to imagine a team with a strong pitching infrastructure looking at Mize's ingredients and seeing a midrotation starter, potentially at a relative discount.

It has been a long and bumpy road for Soroka, who finished sixth in Cy Young voting as a 21-year-old with the Braves way back in 2019. Three Achilles surgeries derailed his ascent, pushing him firmly into "remember that guy?" territory. But Soroka signed a one-year deal with the Nats in 2025 and pitched well enough to earn a midseason trade to the Cubs and another one-year pact, this time for $7.5 million with Arizona. Soroka had a few injury stutter-steps with the D-backs but generally put together a productive season, showcasing enough meaningful changes (lower arm slot, added a cutter) to convince a team to give him multiple years.

The Rays signed Martinez to a one-year deal just before spring training this season with modest hopes that he could provide the pitching staff with some stability and the clubhouse with veteran leadership and good vibes. The well-traveled right-hander far exceeded expectations on and off the field, as he quickly emerged as everyone's favorite teammate while thriving in the rotation, making his first All-Star Game and finishing with a 3.10 ERA that ranked sixth among qualified AL starters. Exceptional command and a fantastic changeup enable Martinez to stifle opponents despite having one of the lowest strikeout rates in the league (15.1%). It'll be fascinating to see if his outstanding clubhouse reputation and late-career breakout earn him a multiyear deal.

With nearly 500 major-league innings under his belt, we've got a pretty good idea of what to expect from Imanaga. He throws a boatload of strikes and can get a healthy amount of whiffs despite below-average velocity, but he is one of the most homer-prone pitchers in the league. No pitcher has allowed more dingers than Imanaga (93!) over the past three seasons, which makes his run prevention rather volatile. That Imanaga has served up that many long balls and still has a 3.45 career ERA speaks to his terrific pitchability, and he has been largely durable since arriving stateside, so there's real value to be had here — especially if he lands in the right ballpark.

This is a funky one. San Diego had a $14 million option on Pivetta for 2027, but if the Padres had activated it, Pivetta would've received an $18 million player option for 2028. Essentially, the Padres would've been committing two years and $32 million to a starter who was limited to 34 ⅔ regular-season innings in 2026. San Diego opted not to do that, and that's why Pivetta is on this list.

It helps that he looked like himself upon his return from injury, working to a 2.86 ERA and 1.01 FIP across eight regular-season starts. The fastball velocity and carry were both there, granting Pivetta a ton of chase above the zone. When healthy, Pivetta is the type of character qualified to handle a postseason start. We're just a bit iffy on the health part.

What a story. The former first-rounder refurbished his career across three seasons in Japan, then made his stateside return last winter, inking a one-year deal with the Nationals. Griffin quickly blossomed into Washington's best hurler, thanks to great command and a kitchen-sink mix. D.C. dealt him to Cleveland at the deadline, and Griffin regressed a tick but generally comported himself well. There's enough here, between the durability and the left-handedness, to command two years. If some team can conjure more velocity out of Griffin, though, he goes from a nice rotation piece to a real playoff starter.

A year ago, France looked dangerously close to the end. He'd latched on with the 2025 Blue Jays but earned just one start and four plate appearances in that World Series. Then France snagged a minor-league deal with San Diego in spring training and proceeded to author the most productive season of his career. He popped 21 bombs, finished sixth in the NL with a .295 average and added outstanding defense at first base. Whether that's enough to earn him a two-year deal remains to be seen, but remember: It takes only one team to believe in the bounce-back.

What a tumultuous and eventful tenure it was for Bohm in the City of Brotherly Love: an All-Star selection, five trips to October, three seasons with a batting average .280 or higher. He is flawed, infuriating, inspiring and occasionally productive. Bohm's go-ahead big fly in wild-card Game 2 felt like an appropriate capper to his time in Philadelphia.

So what kind of player is this guy moving forward? Bohm doesn't chase that much, rarely strikes out and squares the ball up a ton. Despite his size, that contact isn't always firm and definitely isn't at optimal angles. Defensively, he's a bad but playable third baseman who looked better than expected after a midseason move to first. He should sign with the Rockies, hang out with his old friend Mickey Moniak and win a batting title in Coors Field's expansive pastures.

Did you know that from Aug. 1 on, Bohm had a higher wRC+ than Junior Caminero?

Young center fielders coming off down years

Varsho was a key cog for a 2025 Blue Jays club that came within inches of a parade. Go watch his left-on-left homer against Blake Snell from Game 1. Sadly, the stocky Wisconsinite's bat regressed in '26 and got even worse after a deadline deal to the Astros. Varsho's calling card — a phenomenal outfield glove — held firm, giving his profile a slightly higher floor than the two center fielders listed below him. Offensively, though, there are red flags everywhere. His foot speed, bat speed and barrel rate all declined precipitously. Then again, it's a weak market for center fielders, and Varsho can definitely still play the position.

The Mets acquired the tantalizing, injury-plagued toolshed last winter as part of their roster reshuffle. Unfortunately (and unsurprisingly) Robert missed two-and-a-half months due to a spooky-sounding ailment: lumbar spine disc herniation. He came back two weeks before the deadline and raked, but not enough for anybody to take a chance on him. New York offloaded him at the waiver deadline to the Orioles, who were trying to make a late playoff push. But after three games with the Birds, Robert got injured once more, this time with a hamstring issue. Baltimore held a $20 million option for 2027, which the team declined.

Robert, when healthy, has a relatively high floor, given his skills in center. Theoretically, that should give him the leeway from a playing time perspective to get his bat right. The issue with that approach is that if Robert hits the shelf, it throws the whole thing sideways. We predict a one-year deal that allows him the opportunity to rebuild his value.

Grisham was primed to hit the open market coming off a career year last winter, but then the Yankees extended him the qualifying offer. He gleefully accepted, then proceeded to deliver a frustrating and odd 2026. We'll get to the offensive profile in a second, but the headline on Grisham is that he's no longer a viable defender in center. Among the 29 players who logged at least 500 innings in center this season, Grisham ranked dead last in both Fielding Run Value (FRV) and Outs Above Average (OAA). He also rated as the second-slowest every-day center fielder. The eye test, as Yankees fans know, backed up that data.

That development pokes a massive hole in Grisham's profile, even though there's still a lot to like about his bat. He never chases, rarely whiffs, walks a ton and squares the ball up a lot. But Grisham's patience often borders on passivity, which is why his batting average so often tickles the Mendoza Line. His motor and focus also came into question at various times throughout his Yankees tenure.

For Grisham to get multiple years, one of two things needs to happen: Either a club has to believe, for some reason, that it can refurbish Grisham's athleticism and squeeze a few more viable years out of him in center. Or a team has to be particularly bullish on Grisham's bat, viewing him as productive enough to carry an every-day corner outfield spot, despite his shortcomings against left-handed pitching.

Kenley Jansen, Craig Kimbrel and Aroldis Chapman are often grouped together as the ultimate triumvirate of millennial closers, and rightfully so. But the similarly aged Iglesias has also been a spectacular game-ender for nearly a decade now without much fanfare, exemplified by his making his first All-Star Game at age 36. He's back on the open market after another year of handling ninth innings with aplomb, and he would represent an upgrade at closer for plenty of teams. The downward velocity trend is concerning — Iglesias' heater averaged 94 mph in 2026, down from the 96-97 range he resided in a few years ago — but his secondary stuff supports a profile worthy of high-leverage opportunities.

The first season of Pederson's two-year deal with Texas was a downright disaster (77 wRC+), but the second was quietly stellar (128 wRC+), albeit primarily in a platoon role. Considering Pederson's complete incompetence against lefty arms and nearly nonexistent defensive value — in 2026, he appeared in just 13 games at first base and four in right field with the Rangers — this ranking might be a bit generous. But Pederson still crushes right-handed pitching and is a highly regarded clubhouse presence who should draw interest from contenders.

Many, including Stephenson himself, expected the longtime Reds backstop to be dealt at the trade deadline, but Stephenson stayed put for the second half to (likely) finish his lengthy stint in the organization after being drafted out of high school in 2015. Stephenson has been an above-average hitter the past three seasons (107 wRC+), providing some solid pop and drawing a healthy number of walks. His defensive profile is a bit more split, as he rates as an excellent blocker but a poor framer and does not control the running game well. There are flaws here, but for teams seeking an every-day catcher, Stephenson's plus makeup and solid bat make him an intriguing free-agent alternative to Jeffers.

Blocked by Yadier Molina in St. Louis early in his career, Kelly enjoyed a lengthy stint as the D-backs' primary backup before bouncing to the Tigers, Rangers and Cubs. He found a new gear offensively with Chicago, posting a career-best 115 wRC+ in 2025 and recording a career-high 425 plate appearances in 2026. While injuries and inconsistency have cut into his playing time over the years and his defense is more good than great, Kelly's bat has trended favorably and would be welcomed in a lot of lineups.

36. Kevin Gausman, SP, 36 37. Robbie Ray, SP, 35

In the days leading up to the previous MLB lockout, Gausman and Ray each inked five-year free-agent contracts — Gausman with the Blue Jays for $110 million and Ray with the Mariners for $115 million. Gausman didn't miss a start and became a fan favorite in Toronto before being dealt to the Cubs at this year's trade deadline, while Ray underwent Tommy John surgery and was traded twice during his deal. It's clear with hindsight which contract worked out better, but this duo now reenter the market with similar value as veteran workhorses who could be quite useful to a bunch of teams during the regular season but probably shouldn't be counted on to start postseason games anymore.

An oft-injured backend arm earlier in his career, Boyd has hit his stride in his mid-30s as a crafty southpaw starter who is ultra-tough on lefty bats. His excellent changeup headlines a repertoire light on velocity but deep enough to keep hitters guessing. As a competent left-hander and stellar clubhouse presence — two traits all teams covet — Boyd should have plenty of suitors.

May's unsightly 4.70 ERA in 2026 didn't mean he had to settle for a prove-it deal like he did last winter (one year, $12.5 million with St. Louis). There was reason for optimism about his chances of commanding more dollars this time after he set career highs in starts (31) and innings pitched (145 ⅔) while restoring his velocity to the 96-97-mph range. It's concerning that multiple organizations renowned for pitching development (Dodgers, Red Sox, Brewers) struggled to get the most out of May, but this is still a relatively young (29) pitcher with intriguing raw stuff.

The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters developed two of the best Japanese players to ever come stateside in Yu Darvish and Shohei Ohtani. In 2025, Itoh became the first Fighters pitcher since Darvish in 2007 to win the Sawamura Award for best starting pitcher in NPB, leading the league in innings pitched (196 ⅔ across 27 starts) by a wide margin (second-most was 175 ⅓) with a 2.75 ERA. He regressed across the board in 2026, however, somewhat damaging his stock in advance of an expected posting and jump to MLB. At 5-foot-9, 187 pounds, Itoh is not exactly an imposing physical presence, and his velocity is well below average for a right-hander. Still, talent evaluators are enamored with Itoh's pitchability and deep pitch mix, so he could net a multiyear deal from a team seeking rotation upgrades.

A reliable utilityman and bat off the bench, Sosa never eclipsed 300 plate appearances in his five years in Philly. Might another team view him as a starter and pay him accordingly? Perhaps, but we think a contender wins the bidding here. Sosa is a chase-happy walk-hater, but he can really pick it and has good feel for the barrel. He's also a winning player, one who could serve as the weak side of an infield platoon in the right situation.

Dubón emerging as a legitimately good defensive shortstop after eight seasons of admirable utility work qualifies as one of the more surprising, under-the-radar developments of 2026. The affable Honduran also had a nice year with the bat, leaning heavily into a high-contact, low-whiff approach. We have him behind Sosa because (1) he's older, (2) there's less offensive juice, and (3) we're skeptical the industry views him as a no-doubt, elite option at short. Still, this is a really helpful piece, one the Braves might well bring back on a low-AAV, multiyear deal.

From 2022 to 2025, Abreu was one of the most valuable relievers in the big leagues, a bona fide strikeout machine whose wicked fastball-slider combo overwhelmed hitters with regularity. Had he sustained that level of performance in his platform season, he might be 10-15 spots higher on this list. Instead, his velocity dipped and his control evaporated in 2026. His walk rate ballooned to an untenable 15.3%, and his ERA climbed to 3.73, a big jump from the 2.30 he posted over the prior four seasons. The stuff is still quite nasty, so it wouldn't be surprising to see Abreu net a multiyear contract, but there's work to be done here.

44. Alex Vesia, RP, 30 45. JoJo Romero, RP, 30

Only four southpaw relievers threw at least 50 innings with an ERA under 3.50 in each of the past three seasons: Morejón, Braves fireman Dylan Lee and these two. Vesia gets the edge over Romero just because he has done it in big spots for a juggernaut Dodgers team year after year after year. Vesia elicits a ton of whiffs and chases with his high-ride four-seamer, but he loses the zone too often to consider him in the upper echelon of relievers.

Romero, meanwhile, etched his name into October history with three scoreless innings against the Dodgers in the NLCS, including a two-inning outing in the Game 4 clincher . Romero is also something of a Shohei Ohtani kryptonite; the four-time MVP is 1-for-10 against the southpaw.

A pair of arm injuries (rotator cuff, Tommy John) robbed Phillips of a year and a half, but he returned this season and looked like his typical effective self. He strikes out a lot of dudes and hardly walks anybody — probably the two most important things a reliever can do. Phillips is downright nails against righties, thanks to a mind-bending sweeper that had a .059 average against this season. The medical history is less than encouraging, but Phillips seems to be past that now, as much as any hurler can be.

Ward appeared as high as No. 8 on our in-season free-agent rankings , but he plummeted down the list amid a horrific second half. After a deadline deal sent the righty-swinging outfielder from Baltimore to Seattle, Ward went a disastrous 11-for-88 with no doubles, no homers and just one triple. His substandard defense didn't help matters. For whatever reason, Ward completely altered his profile in 2026, trading power (dude hit 36 homers in 2025) for patience (no qualified hitter chased less in 2026). That makes him a total mystery moving forward, and the first question from any interested ballclub has to be "Uh, Taylor, what kind of hitter are you, exactly?"

Like fine wine. The 2022 NL MVP's second act as a southpaw-destroyer has been quite the development. Goldschmidt finished 2026 in the top 10th percentile in nearly every meaningful rate category against left-handed pitching. That's why, one month after his 39th birthday, the seven-time All-Star led off for the Yankees in Game 1 of the wild-card round against the Red Sox. Given his age and specific role, nobody is giving Goldy multiple years, but this is still a very helpful player whom the Mets will be happy to add to their lineup.

There's little that's overwhelming or sexy about Bell's profile at this point. He's a platoon-neutral, switch-hitting DH who doesn't do anything at an elite level. But if you need someone to put together professional at-bats and end the season with a league-average line, this is your dude. You won't win a World Series or reach October because of Bell, but you can certainly do it with him. After he logged a productive 2026 in Minnesota, expect another fringe contender of that ilk to settle for Bell. They could do a whole lot worse.

Retirement, for the veteran slugger, is certainly in play. After a renaissance with Toronto in 2025, Springer came crashing back to Earth, and his final week of 2026 was handled as if the cleats might be hung up. If the four-time All-Star wants to keep going, though, he should be able to find a gig as a bench bat and part-time DH. Springer is just a year removed from a seventh-place MVP finish, after all.

51. J.P. Crawford, SS, 32 52. Ramon Laureano, OF, 32 53. Tyrone Taylor, OF, 32 54. Nathaniel Lowe, 1B, 31 55. Eric Lauer, SP, 32 56. AJ Minter, RP, 33 57. Gregory Soto, RP, 32 58. Antonio Senzatela, RP, 32 59. David Peterson, SP, 31 60. Jack Flaherty, SP, 31
