articles.title: MLB Teams Have Spent $1B+ on Free Agency Contracts Ahead of Potential Lockout
articles.summary: The current collective bargaining agreement between MLB and the MLBPA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on December 1, but a potential lockout hasn't stopped teams from spending in free agency.
articles.body:
The current collective bargaining agreement between MLB and the MLBPA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on December 1, but a potential lockout hasn't stopped teams from spending in free agency.

In fact, there's been a flurry of signings since the World Series ended, to the point that teams have already accounted for $1.2 billion spent:

A good chunk of that $1.2 billion (37.5 percent, to be exact) is attributed to the New York Mets' signing of left-handed starting pitcher Tarik Skubal to a nine-year, $450 million contract.

As of Nightengale's report, five players have signed deals worth $80 million or more.

The Chicago Cubs made a pair of big moves, agreeing to terms with left-handed starting pitcher Trevor Rogers (five years, $120 million) and corner outfielder Teruaki Sato (six years, $120 million), per ESPN's Jeff Passan.

The Baltimore Orioles and starting pitcher Freddy Peralta agreed on a five-year, $125 million contract, per Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic. The Toronto Blue Jays and right-handed starter Kaima Taira also agreed on a five-year, $80 million deal, according to the New York Post 's Jon Heyman .

All of this is going down as the lockout looms. The main sticking point between MLB and MLBPA remains the league's desire to implement a salary cap (and floor) and MLBPA's steadfast resistance against it.

MLB's most recent proposal lists a $180.2 million floor and a $258.2 million cap for the 2028 season, with the 2027 campaign remaining uncapped, per MLB.com's Mark Feinsand .

Per ESPN's Jorge Castillo , commissioner Rob Manfred said the league "will not compromise" regarding the implementation of a cap and floor. MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer said a cap is a "nonstarter."

In the meantime, teams, players and agents are doing business like there's no tomorrow. In a way there may not be soon enough if a lockout happens, which would stop the flurry of free agent signings until a CBA is reached.

Free agency will be intact for at least one more week, though, and one can surmise we'll be seeing more big signings before the clock strikes midnight on Dec. 2.

articles.title: Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s Potential Landing Spots Updated in New MLB Rumors amid Yankees Buzz
articles.summary: The Jazz Chisholm Jr. market is reportedly heating up.
articles.body:
The Jazz Chisholm Jr. market is reportedly heating up.

According to FanSided's Robert Murray , "There are multiple teams, including the Washington Nationals, currently engaged with Chisholm."

Jim Bowden of The Athletic added that "the door has not been shut on a reunion" between the second baseman and New York Yankees.

Forecasting MLB's Biggest 2027 Bombshells 😲

Chisholm, 28, hit .231 with 19 homers, 55 RBI, 69 runs, 41 stolen bases, a .711 OPS and 1.7 WAR for the Yankees this past season. While that's solid offensive production out of a second baseman, it was a major step down from his excellent 2025 (31 homers, .813 OPS).

At his best, Chisholm provides a solid bat, defensive versatility (alongside second base he's also played third base and in the outfield during his career) and speed on the basepaths.

But Chisholm's mentality and decision-making at times have also drawn criticism .

There was his costly throwing error in Game 2 of the ALDS and defiant response to the gaffe after the game:

Or taking the field with a lollipop in his mouth .

And his comments on hustling in Aug. 2025 raised some eyebrows.

"Play at 70 percent: Defense, offense, running, everything," he told the Associated Press. "Stay healthy. You don't overswing. You don't swing and miss as much, and you're a great player at 70 percent."

There was some practical logic in those remarks, given the grueling nature of a 162-game season and the importance of not pressing. But Chisholm nonetheless has a way of occasionally drawing the wrong sort of attention on himself, a factor any interested team will have to take into account.

articles.title: The Padres, Phillies, Astros and Rangers need to hurry up and make some offseason moves
articles.summary: Whether in free agency or via trade, these 4 teams need to get in on the hot stove action before transactions freeze on Dec. 1.
articles.body:
Time is running out for major-league teams to improve their rosters before the expected lockout freezes transactional activity at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Add some semblance of a pause (in theory) for Thanksgiving, and urgency is ramping up for front offices to finalize deals, whether in free agency or via trade.

A handful of teams have already made noteworthy moves during this abbreviated hot stove season . The New York Mets made the biggest splash with their historic agreement with lefty ace Tarik Skubal , added to their infield by signing veteran Paul Goldschmidt and even secured a key member of their young core for the long haul, agreeing to an eight-year extension with outfielder A.J. Ewing .

In the American League, the Boston Red Sox made the first big statement in free agency with the signing of Jake Bauers coming off his breakout campaign and championship run with the Milwaukee Brewers. The New York Yankees have been busy rebuilding their bullpen, retaining closer David Bednar via qualifying offer as well as adding old friend Jonathan Loáisiga and funky lefty Brent Suter to the mix. The Toronto Blue Jays added to their rotation with a five-year deal with Japanese hurler Kaima Taira .

The Minnesota Twins have been surprisingly active, following catcher Ryan Jeffers' accepting the qualifying offer with a hefty, two-year deal with veteran frontline arm Sonny Gray . The Seattle Mariners and Kansas City Royals linked up on a trade that sent All-Star third baseman Maikel Garcia to Seattle in exchange for three big-league arms headlined by Bryce Miller. The Chicago White Sox shook up their pitching staff with the signing of right-hander Dustin May and the trade of Luis Castillo and Davis Martin to Colorado . The Detroit Tigers extended right-hander Troy Melton and added a pair of intriguing arms in Emilio Pagán and former AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil .

The National League has been far quieter by comparison beyond Queens, but the Chicago Cubs got in on the action with a five-year, $120 million deal with starting pitcher Trevor Rogers quickly followed by a six-year, $120 million deal with Japanese slugger Teruaki Satō . The Los Angeles Dodgers added to their bench with the acquisition of former No. 1 draft pick Royce Lewis , and the Atlanta Braves got the bullpen market moving with their signing of Evan Phillips to a three-year deal . The Brewers said goodbye to Bauers and added to their bullpen with a trade for bounce-back candidate Ryan Walker from San Francisco.

While these clubs are surely still scouring the free-agent and trade markets for potential upgrades, they can feel good about having accomplished some portion of their offseason objectives before pencils down on Dec. 1. Meanwhile, a boatload of other teams have yet to complete a meaningful transaction.

Here's a look at four notable clubs that have been eerily quiet thus far, plus what their first major moves could be before action grinds to a halt.

After missing out in the Skubal sweepstakes, the Padres must pivot to reconstructing their rotation without the tantalizing possibility of a two-time Cy Young Award winner in his prime headlining the unit. FanGraphs projects San Diego's current starting staff as the weakest in the majors, even behind the perpetual cellar-dwellers in the category, the Colorado Rockies. There's some comfort in knowing that the bullpen projects as one of the strongest in the majors, even without free agent Adrian Morejon, but it's difficult to feel optimistic about the Padres' chances of competing in the National League until we see how their rotation comes together. Making progress on that front before Dec. 1 would be a welcome development, particularly as new team owners Jose E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones look to build some goodwill with the fan base.

The Padres added right-hander Ryan Weiss on a one-year deal a few weeks ago, but Weiss still has a lot to prove; his Astros stint following a successful run pitching in South Korea did not go especially well in the majors or minors. The Padres have done well to get the most out of pitchers who don't wield premium stuff, so Weiss could be a worthwhile contributor, but handing him a guaranteed rotation spot at this stage feels like a poor Plan A.

As for more ambitious additions to the pitching staff, a reunion with Michael King would be an encouraging first step, but that alone would hardly feel sufficient. There's still an abundance of free-agent starting pitchers at whom San Diego should be taking a close look. May's three-year, $52.5 million deal with the White Sox suggests this portion of the market could be more expensive than anticipated. Even so, San Diego should consider short-term deals for hurlers such as Tyler Mahle, Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga or Clay Holmes. Whatever combination of arms the Padres target — and whether or not they can keep King — it's an inescapable reality that additions on the mound are necessary.

Philadelphia is a club to watch in the coming days for one glaring reason: right field. This has been an enormous weak spot for the Phillies since Nick Castellanos began to decline a few years ago, and Adolis García turned out to be a flop as Philadelphia's first post-Castellanos attempt to plug the position.

Philadelphia arrived at this offseason fresh off another disappointing (and brief) postseason appearance with right field still unaddressed — and the top two free-agent hitters both being corner outfielders in Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena. As such, the question is simple: Can president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski land one of these big bats over the next week?

It will be fascinating to see if Suzuki or Arozarena — super-agent Scott Boras' next top free agent with Skubal having signed — will find new homes, in Philly or elsewhere, in the coming days.

Second or third base is also a point of interest for Philadelphia, with Alec Bohm expected to land elsewhere in free agency. This winter's third-base market is somewhat limited, but free agency offers far more options at the keystone. A run at Brandon Lowe or Jazz Chisholm Jr. or bringing back Luis Arraez could make sense, with Bryson Stott and his terrific glove sliding to third base.

It took a while, but Houston finally has its new leadership structure in place, with general manager Randy Flores and manager Brad Ausmus. Now what? Normally if you just won the division and have the unanimous AL MVP , you'd be feeling pretty good about your situation. But the Astros were the worst division winner in league history, at 81-81, and they have a ton of uncertainty up and down the roster.

Many of the questions that went unresolved last offseason are now even more pressing in Houston. A complicated infield logjam remains, with Alvarez's rightful claim of full-time DH responsibilities leaving five players (Christian Walker, Jose Altuve, Jeremy Peña, Carlos Correa, Isaac Paredes) for four spots. Whether Flores rolls into spring training with this messy and expensive quintet or tries to sort it out before the lockout is one of the bigger questions looming over this team. There are also significant holes in the outfield and on the mound that need to be addressed.

These are not small tasks for Flores as he begins leading a baseball operations department for the first time, and this unusually compressed offseason isn't going to make things any easier.

One of the spiciest early offseason rumors was that the Rangers intended to explore trading star shortstop Corey Seager , even with Seager owed $155 million over the next five years and wielding a no-trade clause. This was all the more compelling after reports that Texas tried to trade Jacob deGrom under similar circumstances at the August trade deadline. If Texas could find a trade partner and a suitable landing spot for Seager, that would ease some payroll and open the door for top prospect Sebastian Walcott to break through to the majors as soon as next season. And with a paucity of impact hitters available in free agency, Seager's bat could still fetch high value in a trade from clubs seeking offensive upgrades.

The Seager rumors seem to have quieted in recent weeks, but that they surfaced in the first place makes the Rangers a team to monitor in the coming days. Texas was far from the only disappointing AL West team in 2026, and there is enough talent on this roster to believe a push for a postseason spot is plausible with the right tweaks. Were the Seager (and deGrom) rumors an indication of a willingness to take a step backward? Or could Texas hold onto its biggest names and add around them in hopes of contending? The Rangers' roster-building has been strange at various intervals since their 2023 World Series run, so these next few days could be illuminating for their direction in 2027.

articles.title: New Yankees Rumors on Adrian Morejon as 'Many' Suitors Emerge amid MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The New York Yankees are interested in relief pitcher Adrián Morejón in free agency, according to Jon Heyman of the New York Post.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees are interested in relief pitcher Adrián Morejón in free agency, according to Jon Heyman of the New York Post .

Per Heyman, the Yankees are among "many" potential suitors for Morejón on the free agent market. Some teams view him as a starter as well.

Morejón chose to test free agency after declining the San Diego Padres' one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer on Nov. 17.

Forecasting MLB's Biggest 2027 Bombshells 😲

He spent each of his first eight MLB seasons on the Padres but may be headed towards a change of scenery.

Morejón didn't have a consistent role in San Diego's bullpen to begin his tenure with the club, appearing in just 50 combined games from 2019-23. He thrived after receiving more opportunities in 2024, though.

In 211 total appearances since the beginning of the 2024 season, Morejón has compiled a 2.58 ERA while averaging 10.0 strikeouts per nine innings. He earned his first All-Star nod in 2025.

The 27-year-old is coming off a 2026 campaign in which he posted a 2.83 ERA, racking up 107 strikeouts compared to 28 walks in 86.0 innings of work. Opposing batters hit just .205 against him.

The Yankees have been focused on addressing their relief pitching this offseason, as general manager Brian Cashman referred to the bullpen as the team's "main priority" in free agency on Nov. 13.

Closer David Bednar accepted the qualifying offer to return to New York on Nov. 17 before the Bronx Bombers brought back relievers Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga on new contracts.

The Yankees also agreed to a one-year deal with left-handed relief pitcher Brett Suter on Tuesday.

As New York looks to make a fourth consecutive playoff appearance in 2027, Morejón is reportedly on the team's radar.

articles.title: Baltimore Orioles finally spend big on a free-agent pitcher, signing Freddy Peralta for $125 million
articles.summary: For the first time under president of baseball operations Mike Elias, the Orioles have agreed to a multiyear contract with a free-agent starting pitcher.
articles.body:
For the first time under president of baseball operations Mike Elias, the Baltimore Orioles have agreed to a multiyear contract with a free-agent starting pitcher.

Two-time All-Star Freddy Peralta is headed to Camden Yards on a five-year, $125 million deal . The deal does not include opt-outs or deferrals. The gregarious 30-year-old Dominican slots into the top of a rotation that finished the 2026 season ranked 17th in ERA, 22nd in strikeout rate and 26th in WHIP. Peralta's signing was part of a flurry of pitching moves from Monday night into Tuesday that saw Kaima Taira sign with the Blue Jays (5/80), Kris Bubic sign with the Guardians (1/17.5) and former Oriole Trevor Rogers sign with the Cubs (5/120).

Baltimore will recoup a compensatory draft pick because of Rogers' departure and will not cede one by signing Peralta. Rogers received and declined a qualifying offer from the Orioles, but Peralta was ineligible for the QO after being dealt midseason.

It's also worth noting that none of the aforementioned deals were as lucrative as Peralta's. Beside Tarik Skubal's paradigm-shattering, nine-year, $450 million pact , Peralta's contract represents the largest commitment to any player so far in this free-agent cycle . Barring a surprise windfall for Seiya Suzuki, Randy Arozarena or Michael King, that's likely to hold true for the remainder of this most bizarre MLB offseason.

That $125 million figure would have been difficult to envision at the August trade deadline, when Peralta, after a disastrous few months with the Mets, was dealt to Tampa Bay. Very little in 2026 had gone right for the nine-year vet after a January swap sent him from Milwaukee to Queens.

Peralta was considered one of the more reliable arms in the sport after a half-decade of borderline-elite performance with the Brewers. But instead of propping up New York's starting staff, he was a massive reason for the club's dramatic downfall. With the Mets, Peralta's ERA and home run rate skyrocketed. His fastball velocity and strikeout rate dipped. And with free agency on the horizon, his future earnings appeared to be dwindling in real time.

The move to Tampa Bay changed everything.

With the Rays, Peralta began throwing his changeup more. He scrapped his full windup, opting to work exclusively from the stretch. His extension and fastball velocity climbed. So, too, did the surface-level numbers; Peralta posted a 3.25 ERA after the trade. And if you remove his first Rays start post-trade (a seven-run stinker at Coors Field), that figure dips to 2.26. Fastball Freddy backed that up with an emphatic, magnificent postseason run: 2.95 ERA across 21 1/3 innings.

Under the hood, however, there are a few causes for concern. Peralta's strikeout rate didn't climb after he left the Mets. His significantly more palatable ERA in Tampa was almost certainly a product of playing in front of an elite defense instead of an average one. Peralta's batting average on balls in play was .315 as a Met and .235 as a Ray.

But ostensibly, Peralta's late-season resurgence was enough to woo the Orioles, who made him the highest-paid pitcher in franchise history.

Since taking over Baltimore's baseball operations department in November 2018, Mike Elias has generally maintained a conservative, cautious approach in free agency in general and toward free-agent pitching specifically. That continued even once private equity tycoon David Rubenstein purchased the club in March 2024. Under Elias' stewardship, the O's dispensed one-year deals to starters Chris Bassitt ($18.5M), Charlie Morton ($15M), Tomoyuki Sugano ($13M), Zach Eflin ($10M) and Kyle Gibson ($10M). Unsurprisingly, none of those risk-averse signings resulted in All-Star appearances, Cy Young votes or postseason wins.

In 2026, however, the Orioles were aggressive in retaining their own hurlers, agreeing to extensions with both Shane Baz (five years, $68 million) and Kyle Bradish (five years, $90 million). Those came on the heels of a massive investment in free-agent slugger Pete Alonso, who joined last winter for five years and $155 million.

And so, Peralta's signing is both a continuation of Baltimore's new, more indulgent way of life under Rubenstein's stewardship and an ideological break from Elias' established modus operandi. It's a sign that after two straight years of missing the postseason, Baltimore is hell-bent on winning in the short term.

Elias' job, frankly, might depend on it.

articles.title: Blue Jays add entertaining mystery box Kaima Taira to their rotation on 5-year, $80 million deal
articles.summary: Exactly how well Taira's stuff and build will translate is impossible to predict, but the diminutive righty offers something totally unique in MLB today.
articles.body:
The Toronto Blue Jays, perpetual free-agency bridesmaids, did not reel in Tarik Skubal earlier this week , despite offering the two-time Cy Young Award winner $420 million over nine years. Thus marked another instance, another winter of Canada's club finishing second on a top-tier free agent. It happened with Juan Soto, with Shohei Ohtani, with Kyle Tucker. For all the commendable aggression shown by Toronto's ownership group over the past few years, for all the dollars offered and committed, it has proven difficult for the Jays to woo the biggest fish to come north of the border.

That frustrating state of play hasn't yet squashed Toronto's willingness and ability to spend.

On Tuesday, the Blue Jays agreed to terms with Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira on a five-year, $80 million contract . The deal includes an opt-out after the third season and contains a $5 million signing bonus. Because Taira is headed stateside from Nippon Professional Baseball, Toronto must also pay a $13.875 million posting fee to Taira's now-former NPB team, the Seibu Lions.

Taira, a 27-year-old right-hander who grew up in Ishigaki, Japan's southernmost city, is not Skubal. But he might be just as interesting. Listed at 5-foot-8 and 220 pounds, Taira is built like a Dutch oven, albeit one with a triple-digit fastball. The undersized hurler matriculated into NPB out of high school as a fourth-round draft pick. Debuting at 19 years old in 2019, Taira initially worked as a reliever before transitioning to Seibu's rotation for the 2023 campaign. He showed well that season, posting a 2.40 ERA across 150 innings. A forearm issue derailed his 2024 season and eventually bumped him back into the bullpen, where he stayed for 2025.

This past year, Seibu gave Taira another chance to start, and the stout flamethrower took the opportunity by the horns. Taira threw 146 innings across 22 starts with a 1.36 ERA, a 24.8% strikeout rate and a 7.9% walk rate. Yuri Karasawa of Japan Ball, the industry's premier English-language NPB resource, mentioned on a recent episode of "Baseball Bar-B-Cast" that continuing as a starter was an absolute must for Taira as he made the transition to MLB.

He seems primed to get that opportunity in Toronto.

Taira will join a rotation helmed by AL Cy Young runner-up Dylan Cease, whose first season in Toronto proved to be a magnificent success. Midseason trade addition José Soriano and 2025 postseason hero Trey Yesavage also figure to retain rotation spots, barring injury. Cody Ponce and Spencer Arrighetti will battle it out for the No. 5 spot, with the other joining a long list of upper-level prospect depth options such as Ricky Tiedemann, Jake Bloss, Johnny King and Nolan Perry.

Accordingly, expect Toronto to now turn its offseason focus to its offense, a unit that disappointed massively last season after a rip-roaring 2025. Seiya Suzuki, Randy Arozarena and Jazz Chisholm Jr. are all reasonable fits still available on the market .

Exactly how well Taira's stuff and build will translate to the stateside game is impossible to predict, but the diminutive righty immediately becomes something of a statistical outlier. San Diego Padres reliever Yuki Matsui was the only pitcher in MLB last season to measure in at 5-foot-8 or shorter. The only pitcher that short who recorded double-digit starts over the past decade is former Blue Jay Marcus Stroman.

In that sense, the odds are stacked against Toronto's $80 million fire hydrant, who also lacks a track record of shouldering a full starter's workload.

But like Stroman, Taira is an atypical athlete. He's remarkably athletic on the mound and when fielding his position. His lower-half strength and flexibility are downright preposterous. Taira's "drop-and-drive" mechanics also mean he gets an outrageous amount of extension for his size and is ridiculously low to the ground at pitch release, both of which create an extreme, difficult-to-hit, flat angle on his heater. At the top of its velocity range, Taira's heater should miss tons of bats in and above the zone, a la peak Craig Kimbrel, Spencer Strider, Sonny Gray or Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

There is, however, a concern that Taira, like some Japanese pitchers before him, might struggle in transitioning from the smaller, tackier and higher-seamed NPB ball to the larger, less-tacky and flatter-seamed MLB ball. As noted by Marquee's Lance Brozdowski in his recent deep dive on Taira , Japanese pitchers tend to lose a noticeable amount of horizontal and vertical movement on their fastballs after making the jump.

Taira's deep array of secondary offerings should help mitigate that problem, as should his incredibly unique release point. His splitter, an offering he leaned on heavily in NPB, will help him neutralize left-handed big leaguers and avoid a massive platoon split. But fastball command and velocity will likely determine how successful Taira is with Toronto.

His heater crept up to triple digits at points during his time with the Lions but sat more in the 94-95 range. If he can sustain or increase that velocity while maintaining his command, he should be capable of sticking in the rotation. It's also worth noting that Taira is a dedicated student of the game and runs his own YouTube channel in which he discusses pitching theory, approach, physics and grips.

In total, Taira is a sure-to-be-entertaining mystery box. Nothing else like this exists in MLB right now, and that should quickly make Taira a fan favorite for Jays fans and neutrals alike.

articles.title: Major League Baseball players just called Rob Manfred's bluff with new proposal ahead of lockout | Ian Miller
articles.summary: Major League Baseball players agreed to share media revenues equally across 30 clubs, calling the owners' bluff on competitive balance as lockout looms.
articles.body: In just over one week, the 30 Major League Baseball owners will almost certainly lock players out of team facilities, pull down merchandise from their stores and generally act as though the players' fans pay to see don't exist. There is no requirement that they do this, but it's become common practice for the league and ownership to enforce a "lockout" in hopes of pressuring the players to come to terms. This year's upcoming lockout, as has been widely reported, will revolve around the owners' desire to do a complete revamp of baseball's economic structure. Baseball has no salary cap, unlike the NFL and NBA, which means players can earn whatever the free market decides they're worth. It's up to each ownership group to set a budget for themselves and determine what they're willing to spend. For some, it's worth paying exorbitant "luxury tax" penalties to sign higher-priced players. MLB OWNERS ARE BACK WITH A NEW SALARY CAP PROPOSAL TO SHUT DOWN SPORT EVEN AFTER BREWERS WIN WORLD SERIES For others, like Pittsburgh Pirates owner Bob Nutting, free agency is a once-a-decade experience, meant to sign a player here or there to a two-year contract in order to keep dozens of fans in their seats. But one of the consequences of this free market system is that, unlike sports socialism, it limits franchise valuations. Because potential buyers of organizations in the NBA and NFL have certainty around what the top end of their outlays will be, they can justify paying higher ownership premiums. But in baseball, there's always the concern that fans might care about winning, which could require more spending. That's bad, you see, to care about a competitive sport, as it cuts into profits. ONE OF MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL'S OWNERS JUST DESTROYED THE LEAGUE'S ENTIRE ARGUMENT FOR A LOCKOUT Why these potential buyers don't just invest in other things, if they care so little about winning, is never brought up. But billionaires gonna billionaire, so here we sit in late November 2026, staring at the potential of a canceled 2027 season. Another contention that owners make is that the league cannot achieve competitive balance without the creation of a salary cap. Teams like the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining baseball by signing players and winning, and teams like the New York Mets or Los Angeles Angels are also ruining baseball by signing players and losing. The Milwaukee Brewers, Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays don't exist, and players must limit their earning potential in order to make the Pirates, Rockies, and Marlins happy. Their contention about "competitive balance" is factually wrong, first of all, as numerous analyses have demonstrated that payroll has the same added influence on winning as fielding a pitching staff that induces higher groundball rates. Which is to say, very little added influence. There's also the fact that the Dodgers, for all their spending, are 3-14 since 2008 in the postseason, as far as winning the World Series goes, despite their exorbitant payroll. Or that the Padres, one of baseball's highest spenders over the past five years, have won one game in the NLCS for their troubles. Then there's the Mets, Giants and Angels. Or the Cubs who haven't even reached the NLCS since 2017. Boston has done little since 2018, and the Texas Rangers, from the massive Dallas metroplex, won in 2023 and haven't been back to the playoffs since. Houston won 81 games last year, and the Yankees haven't won the World Series in 17, going on 18, years. All this is to say that there is no competitive balance problem to worry about. Owners have claimed there is anyway. And this week, the player's association called their bluff. If, as the league claims, payroll differences are the cause of the nonexistent competitive balance problems, and that revenue disparities are the cause of those differences, the players just found the answer: share more revenue. The owners recently claimed that sharing more revenue would allow the end of local blackouts, a nonsensical view that is totally unrelated to the actual cause of local blackouts. They also claimed that sharing more media income would close the gap between the rich and poor teams. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE So the players, in a new press release, said, essentially, "Great, we agree." "Today, players reaffirmed their commitment to reaching a fair deal by agreeing to the owners’ proposal to share all MLB media revenues equally across the 30 clubs," their post said. "The MLBPA also maintained its previous proposal to transfer hundreds of millions in additional non-media revenues from high-revenue teams to low-revenue teams, along with critical proposals meant to ensure all subsidies are used by front offices to improve the product on the field. Over the course of the next CBA, the players’ revenue-sharing proposals will increase assistance to low-revenue clubs by over $1 billion." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! And there's the called bluff. Owners don't actually care about competitive balanceor whether a small or big market team wins. They care about a salary cap because it will take a higher percentage of baseball revenue away from the players and redistribute it to them. It's the Zohran Mamdani model. Particularly when considering that the league's proposal would exclude billions in ancillary baseball revenue, such as income from The Battery, a commercial development attached to Truist Park in Atlanta. The supposed "floor" would also include things like player benefits and expenses. Meaning that the supposed ~$171 million salary floor would be substantially lower, roughly $30 million, at least, lower in actual payroll. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Then there's the blackouts issue. A salary cap has nothing to do with local blackouts, but the Players Association's proposal ends that argument too. Redistribute more media revenue from big to small market teams, and end blackouts. Level the media playing field. Just keep a salary cap out of it. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD If the owners were serious about competitive balance, which they of course are not, this would be a major step towards an agreement and a quick lockout. Or none at all. But because this has never been about competitive balance, we'll suddenly see the goalposts move. Quickly. And again, salary cap or no, the cheap teams like the Pirates and Marlins will always spend the bare minimum. Competence is the biggest separator, which is why the Angels have been a disaster, despite having Mike Trout and Shohei Ohtani on the same team, and why the Rockies' big deals have flopped, while the Brewers keep winning. Spending less on players won't fix incompetence. But it will make owners more money, and that's, as always, what they really care about.

articles.title: Revisiting Every Rangers Top Prospect Since 2011: Leody Taveras
articles.summary: Texas Rangers homegrown outfielder Leody Taveras had some iconic moments with the franchise during the 2023 World Series championship run.
articles.body:
Since 2011, MLB has compiled a Top 30 Prospects list for every organization in the league. Some players have turned out to be busts, some have become stars, and others are somewhere in between.

The Texas Rangers haven't exactly been a hotbed for prospect development over the years, but they have had some players who've come through the organization and become key contributors to the big-league club.

In this series, we'll take a look at the Rangers' Top Prospect in every year since 2011 , when the rankings began, and remember the mark, or lack thereof, they've left on the organization's recent history.

Back in 2017, the Top Prospect in the Texas organization was outfielder Leody Taveras, who would go on to become the starting center fielder on the first World Series-winning team in franchise history in 2023.

The 2023 season was Taveras' best with the Rangers and in the Major Leagues as he hit .266 with 14 home runs and 67 RBI while hitting out of the nine hole and playing excellent defense in center field.

Taveras finished with a WAR of 2.9 that season in a year in which Texas made the postseason but just one game.

Despite 2023 being his best season, the story of Taveras with the Rangers begins in July of 2015 when he signed with the team out of the Dominican Republic for an impressive $2.1 million.

At the time, Taveras was considered one of the most athletic prospects available in international free agency.

Following five seasons in the Rangers minor-league system, Taveras made the big-league Opening Day roster in the shortened 2020 season.

During his rookie year, Taveras played in 33 of the 60 games that year, hitting .227 with four home runs and six RBI.

In his first full season in 2021, Taveras appeared in just 49 games but struggled, hitting just .161 with three home runs and nine RBI.

Taveras set the stage for a breakout in 2023 with a strong 2022 season where he hit .261 with five home runs and 34 RBI.

Unfortunately for Taveras, much like a lot of the World Series-winning roster for Texas, he was unable to reach the heights he hit during that run.

In the middle of the 2025 season, the Rangers designated Taveras for assignment, and he has played for a pair of other teams since.

There is no doubt that Taveras did not become what you hope a Top Prospect will be, but his contributions to the World Series title team will not be forgotten.

articles.title: Potential Padres Free Agent Targets After Losing Out on Skubal
articles.summary: The San Diego Padres have lost out on top free agent Tarik Skubal. The southpaw signed a pitcher-record $450 million deal with the New York Mets. With Skubal...
articles.body:
The San Diego Padres have lost out on top free agent Tarik Skubal. The southpaw signed a pitcher-record $450 million deal with the New York Mets . With Skubal now off the board, who are some potential Padres free agent targets in order to build out their roster for the 2027 season and beyond? Here are some signings the club could make that would increase payroll by the same amount as Skubal's deal.

Re-signing Michael King remains an imminent priority. With the news of Trevor Rogers and Freddy Peralta signing elsewhere , the free agent starting pitcher market grows thinner by the hour. King is an easy starter for the Padres to focus on this offseason , having spent the last three seasons with the Friars. He was an ace for two of those seasons, pitching to a 2.95 ERA in 2024 and a 3.21 ERA in '26. 2025 was a tough year for King, with injuries derailing most of his season.

The other top option left on the board is Clay Holmes. The right-hander has been incredibly consistent throughout the last six seasons, posting a sub-4.00 ERA each year. The Mets converted Holmes into a starter in 2025, and he looked phenomenal. Holmes posted a 3.53 ERA over 165 2/3 innings in 2025 before turning in another solid performance in 2026 (3.29 ERA, 101 1/3 IP). New York's coaching staff set Holmes on the right track, but San Diego's elite pitching coach Ruben Niebla could make him even better.

The combination of King and Holmes at the top of the Padres' rotation would instantly elevate it. This is by far the most expensive addition the Friars would make this offseason, but the rotation is in need of it. King is projected to earn a five-year, $140 million deal this offseason while Holmes is expected to sign a three-year, $54 million contract. That eats up almost half of the imaginary $450 million that San Diego has to work with, but it's necessary.

The next move is signing a slugger to man the outfield. Either Randy Arozarena or Seiya Suzuki would work here. That being said, Suzuki is the better option. He's a more complete player than Arozarena, who boasts elite power/speed numbers. Additionally, the Padres have been linked as the favorites to sign Suzuki after the club hosted him last week.

Suzuki has also been one of the most consistent hitters in baseball over the last half-decade. The slugger has hit 20-plus homers in four consecutive seasons and has hit .270 or better in three of the last four years. His defense also improved, with +7 Fielding Run Value and +5 Outs Above Average. Suzuki is projected to sign a four-year, $110 million contract. That's certainly pricey, but it's worth it to bolster the lineup.

With $330 million spent, the Padres then turn to filling out depth. Re-signing Ty France, Adrian Morejon, and Nick Pivetta are all top priorities. France will be worth a three-year, $48 million deal, while Morejon could still potentially sign a team-friendly deal in order to stay in San Diego. After his injury-plagued 2026 campaign, Pivetta probably won't sign until after the lockout, but could return to the Padres on a short-term deal.

Beyond that, signing mid-tier free agents like Shota Imanaga or Foster Griffin would be solid moves that wouldn't cost too much. Perhaps a bench bat or two, though a trade for Jarren Duran to fill out the outfield could be a better decision in that regard. Once the dust settles, the Padres would have a true World Series contender on their hands. With King and Peralta anchoring the rotation alongside perennial stars like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado in the lineup, San Diego might finally bring home a championship.

articles.title: Despite Injury, Marlins Reliever is a Cherished Commodity
articles.summary: Andrew Nardi re-signed with the Fish, even though he likely won't pitch at all in 2027
articles.body:
The Miami Marlins are willing to exercise a little patience when it comes to Andrew Nardi . Even though the left-handed reliever is expected to miss most, if not all, of the 2027 season following elbow surgery, the Fish decided his future value outweighs the immediate cost of keeping him around.

President of baseball operations Peter Bendix decided to tender Nardi a contract for 2027, retaining a pitcher who has experienced plenty of ups and downs during his time in Miami. It is a calculated gamble, but one that makes considerable sense when considering what Nardi has demonstrated when healthy.

Originally selected by Miami in the 16th round of the 2019 MLB Draft, Nardi worked his way through the organization's minor league system before making his major league debut on August 16, 2022. He immediately showed flashes of the strikeout potential that would eventually make him an important bullpen option.

In 13 appearances during his rookie season, Nardi recorded 24 strikeouts in 14 1/3 innings. That represented an impressive introduction, and he continued building on that foundation the following year.

His 2023 campaign represented the high point of his major league career. Nardi appeared in 49 games, posting a 2.67 ERA and a 1.15 WHIP. He established himself as a dependable left-handed option, demonstrating the ability to miss bats and provide valuable innings in the middle of Miami's bullpen.

However, the road became considerably more difficult afterward. The pitcher has been all over the place in terms of his health ever since.

Nardi struggled with injuries and inconsistency in 2024, finishing with a 5.07 ERA across 49 2/3 innings. Still, there were encouraging signs beneath the surface. He struck out 70 batters, averaging 12.7 strikeouts per nine innings, while posting a 3.33 FIP. He also delivered a particularly impressive stretch after returning from an elbow injury, recording a 1.74 ERA in 20 2/3 innings across his final 22 appearances.

Back trouble prevented him from pitching in 2025, making his return to the Opening Day roster in 2026 something of a comeback story. Unfortunately, another injury interrupted that progress. Nardi appeared in just 25 games, recording a 5.16 ERA and 27 strikeouts in 22 2/3 innings before undergoing season-ending left elbow surgery in August.

The 28-year-old southpaw seemingly brings no value to a team that's hoping to bust through the postseason ceiling in the upcoming campaign. But his unavailability won't do manager Clayton McCullough much good in Year 3.

The answer involves both potential and organizational necessity. Nardi is only 28 years old and has accumulated 194 strikeouts in 144 1/3 career innings. More importantly, he represents an experienced left-handed arm in a bullpen that lacks quality southpaw depth.

Without Nardi, Miami has limited healthy left-handed options, making his eventual return particularly valuable. There's also a financial component. The agreement is likely close to the major league minimum, minimizing the financial risk.

The Marlins aren't retaining Nardi because of what he can provide in 2027. They're retaining him because of what he could provide afterward.

For a club trying to build sustainable bullpen depth without spending excessively, that's a gamble worth taking. If Nardi can rediscover his 2023 form, Miami could eventually get a significant return on a relatively inexpensive investment.

articles.title: Luis Ortiz's wife texted him to 'delete the evidence,' in alleged pitch-fixing scheme, per court evidence
articles.summary: The wife of former Guardians pitcher Luis Ortiz allegedly urged him via text message to "delete the evidence" regarding an alleged pitch-fixing scheme in whi...
articles.body:
The wife of former Cleveland Guardians pitcher Luis Ortiz allegedly urged him via text message to "delete the evidence" regarding an alleged pitch-fixing scheme in which Ortiz is accused of intentionally blowing pitches to ensure the outcome of prop bets.

That's according to prosecutor's evidence presented in federal court Tuesday, as reported by ESPN .

Per the report, prosecutors presented text messages from Ortiz's wife, Altagracia Reynoso, from June 27, 2025 reading "what if he's undercover," "what if it's a setup" and "Luis, it's your future."

Reynoso allegedly followed up with texts reading "delete all conversations," "if you can, send the deposit in someone else's name" and "delete the evidence." Ortiz, per court evidence, followed up with a text reading "No, that's not gonna be sent in my name, no."

The texts were written in Spanish and translated to English for presentation in court, according to the report. Ortiz's attorneys declined comment Tuesday, according to the report.

Risking millions to allegedly win thousands

Ortiz and his former Guardians teammate Emmanuel Clase are facing federal trial at a U.S. District Court in Brooklyn over an alleged scheme in which the two pitchers are accused of accepting payments to throw specific pitches during MLB games to ensure the success of prop bets.

They face charges of wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery and money laundering conspiracy. Reynoso does not face charges and has not been accused of wrongdoing. Ortiz and Clase have pleaded not guilty.

Per prosecutors, Ortiz's wife sent the above texts hours after Ortiz pitched in a game for the Guardians and threw one of the pitches in question. Here's that pitch in which Ortiz bounced a ball into the dirt well outside the plate:

That was Ortiz's first pitch of the game in a relief appearance.

Per ESPN , Joshua Mehta, the director of legal and regulatory affairs for FanDuel, testified last week that accounts registered to associates of Clase placed bets on first pitches from the June 27 Guardians game against the Cardinals and a June 15 Guardians game against the Mariners.

Per Mehta, one of those accounts was registered to Enoc Pena, whom government witness testimony states is a close associate of Clase's. Mehta testified that a ball that Ortiz threw outside the strike zone against the Mariners won approximately $12,000 on a prop bet. He also testified that at least five accounts that bet on Ortiz's pitches were suspended in June 2025, according to ESPN.

Ortiz and Clase have been on MLB's "non-disciplinary paid leave" since 2025 and have not played baseball since. Ortiz was in his third full MLB season and playing on a one-year, $782,000 contract at the time he was placed on leave.

Clase was a three-time All-Star and a Cy Young Award finalist in 2024. He was playing on a five-year, $20 million contract and was on track for a lucrative long-term contract extension prior to being placed on leave.

Prosecutors rested their case Tuesday. Per ESPN, the trial is scheduled to resume Monday with closing arguments.

articles.title: Tarik Skubal beat the MLB lockout. Everyone else has a week to go.
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal got his $450 million. Rob Manfred and Bruce Meyer are a week from an MLB lockout, still split on a salary cap. Here's what freezes and what's at...
articles.body:
Tarik Skubal didn't wait to find out what a salary cap would do to his price.

The two-time American League Cy Young Award winner agreed Nov. 22 to a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets, the richest deal ever for a pitcher . He got it done 10 days before baseball is expected to shut down.

Major League Baseball's collective bargaining agreement, the contract that sets the rules between owners and players, expires at 11:59 p.m. ET Dec. 1. Owners are expected to lock out the players the moment it does. Trades and free-agent signings would stop , and teams couldn't even pick up the phone to call the 40-man roster players they employ.

The two sides head into the final week stuck where they've been since May. They traded proposals again on Nov. 23, and neither one budged on the cap. Commissioner Rob Manfred said Nov. 18 he "can't imagine" owners approving a deal without a salary cap and floor. Bruce Meyer, interim executive director of the MLB Players Association , said the league's insistence on a cap shows its "lack of seriousness."

The Los Angeles Dodgers traded for Skubal at the August deadline and never made him an offer. ESPN reported that uncertainty over the next labor deal kept them out of the bidding.

The rest of the free-agent market has a week to get deals done − or spend the winter wondering what their future holds.

10 MLB free agents to watch according to baseball insider

Latest MLB lockout news and where labor talks stand

MLB's offer made Nov. 23, puts more money in younger players' pockets. It doesn't touch the cap.

The minimum salary would jump from $780,000 to $1 million for every player in 2027. Arbitration-eligible players who settle with their teams before a hearing would get an automatic 5% bonus. Each team could also hand one veteran on a one-year deal of $10 million or less a $500,000 signing bonus.

The catch is that all of it comes with the cap.

"The league's proposals today don't add a single dollar in overall player compensation as compared to prior proposals, and once again are expressly conditioned on accepting their salary cap and other anti-player restrictions," Meyer said in a statement.

The union's counter was to take one piece of MLB's plan and drop the rest. Players agreed to split all local media revenue evenly among the 30 teams, an idea MLB had put inside its cap proposal, and said owners can do it without a cap. The union also wants aid to low-revenue teams raised from about $700 million to more than $950 million. It kept its proposal to pay those teams $20 million when they contend.

"The Union's claim that our proposal would negatively impact 'all categories of players' is not accurate," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said.

Nothing has moved on the cap since the owners' meetings. Manfred wrapped those up Nov. 18 without giving an inch. MLB's offer has a $258.2 million cap and a $180.2 million floor starting in 2028, with the current system kept for 2027.

"There's plenty of room for compromise, but there's one thing that I will not compromise," Manfred said.

He said the owners would decide on a lockout "at the last possible moment." He also brushed off the idea that the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, two low-payroll teams, meeting in the World Series means the system works.

"This should not be a once-in-a-decade phenomenon for us," Manfred said.

Meyer told the Boston Globe the union figures players already take home 55% to 56% of the sport's revenue. That's more than the 50-50 split MLB is offering. The league, meanwhile, put out a five-minute video asking fans to back a cap.

"They're talking out of both sides of their mouth," Meyer said.

World Series champions through the years: See MLB's winners since 1996

The sides traded smaller concession on Nov. 20. MLB dropped its plan to keep high school players out of the draft, and the union turned down an international draft.

MLB tweaked its proposal Tuesday, Nov. 24 in the final negotiating session before Thanksgiving.

The union's executive board meets in Scottsdale, Arizona, at the end of the month, right up against the deadline. A lockout would be baseball's 10th work stoppage since 1972.

Tarik Skubal contract and which MLB free agents signed before the lockout

Skubal's deal is the fourth-biggest in MLB history, behind Juan Soto, Shohei Ohtani and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. At $50 million a year, he passes the pitcher record of $43.3 million that Max Scherzer set with the Mets in 2021.

Skubal's $45 million signing bonus will be paid right away, so the lockout can't touch it. Another $30 million is deferred, which is the kind of money MLB's cap plan would ban.

The Mets' projected payroll for next season was already over $340 million before they signed him, according to Cot's Baseball Contracts.

Nobody else has come close. The other notable deals so far:

Paul Goldschmidt: Mets, one year, $8 million

The Seattle Mariners also picked up third baseman Maikel Garcia from the Kansas City Royals in a six-player trade Nov. 18.

The last lockout set off a rush. In 2021, teams handed out more than $1.9 billion in new contracts in the days before it started, and $1.4 billion of it came on the final day.

What freezes when the MLB lockout starts Dec. 2?

The lockout covers every player on a 40-man roster. Signings, trades, waiver claims and releases all stop.

A free agent who is still unsigned on Dec. 2 waits for a new deal, however long that takes.

Minor leaguers who aren't on the 40-man roster carry on as usual. They have their own labor deal, and it stays in force.

What the lockout means for the MLB offseason calendar and Opening Day 2027

The early deadline has already passed. The Winter Meetings, usually the busiest week of the offseason, are set for Dec. 7-9 in San Diego. Few people in the game expect them to happen. In 2021, MLB canceled the meeting and the major league portion of the Rule 5 Draft.

Pitchers and catcher were expected to report to spring training as early as Feb. 9, and position players usually follow about five days later. Spring training games start Feb. 19, and Opening Night is March 24 on Netflix.

How long could the MLB lockout last? Will 2027 games be canceled?

Nobody knows yet. But no games are on the schedule until Feb. 19, so the lockout can run all winter without wiping out one. A growing number of executives expect the season to start around Memorial Day weekend.

The last lockout ran 99 days, from Dec. 2, 2021 to March 10, 2022. Owners waited six weeks, until Jan. 13, to make their first proposal. Opening Day slid from March 31 to April 7, and makeup games saved the full 162-game schedule.

Baseball's earlier lockouts were short and came in the spring. They lasted about two and a half weeks in 1973, 17 days in 1976 and 32 days in 1990. None of them cost a game.

The big stoppage that did cost games was a strike. Owners pushed for a salary cap in 1994, the players walked out and the World Series was canceled.

It's a legal move in which the union stops being a union.

The MLB Players Association would declare that it no longer represents the players and reform as a trade association. With no union, there's no collective bargaining. Players could then sue, arguing that a lockout of non-union workers is an illegal group boycott. Federal law triples the damages in antitrust cases.

The Wall Street Journal reported that MLB is preparing for that possibility. Meyer wouldn't discuss the union's legal options yet. It is a tactic that is floated around every baseball work stoppage.

On Nov. 10, Sens. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., and Mike Lee, R-Utah , introduced a bill to end baseball's century-old antitrust exemption. The union welcomed it.

The bill wouldn't change the lockout though. The Curt Flood Act of 1998 already took player employment out of the exemption, so players can bring antitrust claims over labor matters now. Nobody has tested it, because every round of bargaining since then has ended in a deal.

Why doesn't MLB have a salary cap? Key issues in the lockout fight

Salary cap and floor: Baseball has never had either one. MLB's latest offer is a $258.2 million cap and a $180.2 million floor starting in 2028. Players have refused a cap since the 1994 strike that canceled the World Series.

Revenue split: MLB wants an even 50-50 split. The union says players already get 55% to 56%.

Local TV money: Both sides have proposed splitting local media revenue evenly among the 30 teams. MLB ties it to a cap, and the union wants it without one.

Luxury tax: Teams paid it in 2026 once payroll passed $244 million. The union wants that line raised to $300 million and wants to end the draft-pick penalties.

Tax on low spenders: This is the union's alternative to a floor. Teams that spend too little on payroll would pay it.

Minimum salary: It's $780,000 now. The union wants $1.5 million. MLB offered $1 million for 2027, but only with a cap.

New bonuses: MLB offered a 5% bonus to arbitration players who settle before a hearing, plus a $500,000 bonus for one veteran per team. Meyer said the offers "don't add a single dollar in overall player compensation."

Free agency: Both sides would let players 30 and older become free agents after five years instead of six, and both would end the qualifying offer. MLB ties those changes to a cap.

Contract limits: MLB wants caps on contract length and a ban on deferred money.

The draft: MLB has proposed cutting it from 20 rounds to 12. It dropped its plan to keep high school players out. The union rejected an international draft.

Where they agree: The two sides have made progress on gambling, drug testing and domestic violence policies.

articles.title: The Perfect Fit for Biggest Names Remaining in 2026-27 MLB Free-Agent Class
articles.summary: Though the colossal $450 million Tarik Skubal domino has fallen, most of Major League Baseball's other free agents remain unsigned, searching for the perfect fit—or simply the biggest offer.
articles.body:
Though the colossal $450 million Tarik Skubal domino has fallen, most of Major League Baseball's other free agents remain unsigned, searching for the perfect fit—or simply the biggest offer.

And with an expected lockout just one week away from bringing offseason transactions to a screeching halt, it's likely there will continue to be a flurry of substantial signings in the coming days.

Based on a combination of current roster situations/needs, projected spending and maybe a tiny bit of ballpark splits, we've put together updated perfect fits for the top players still available.

Players are presented in alphabetical order by last name.

Consensus Contract Projections are the average from MLB Trade Rumors , ESPN's Kiley McDaniel and our Tim Kelly . For what it's worth, their consensus on Skubal was nine years, $403M. Not too shabby.

2026 Stats: .281/.381/.484, 26 HR, 79 RBI, 26 SB, 5.7 bWAR

Career Stats : .255/.350/.442, 144 HR, 469 RBI, 157 SB, 22.6 bWAR

Consensus Contract Projection : 4 years, $25.4M AAV

Historically speaking, free-agent outfielders (except for those named Aaron Judge) heading into their age-31 (or older) season don't get contracts of four or more years.

That's because most of the ones in the past decade who have had such contracts—Starling Marte, Lorenzo Cain, Dexter Fowler, Chris Taylor and especially Yoenis Céspedes—were practically unplayable by Year 3, if not sooner. They simply don't age well.

But maybe Randy Arozarena is going to be the exception to that rule.

He has, after all, put together six consecutive seasons of at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases, and just completed the best campaign of his career.

Even if the latter half of the contract goes poorly, maybe he could be the driving force of a team that wins it all in 2027 and/or 2028?

And, well, "desperate to win right now at the cost of a few painfully old-and-expensive years in the 2029-32 timeframe" already describes the Philadelphia Phillies to a T, so what's one more well-compensated, multiple-time All-Star who will be in his mid-30s by the end of his contract?

Provided they can make the finances work, the roster fit could not be more ideal.

Their corner outfield situation has been brutal for half a decade at this point, and they were woefully lacking for right-handed bats worth a darn in 2026. Though Arozarena is hardly a Gold Glover in left field, he'd be a "two birds, one stone" solution for what is already one of the top threats to win the 2027 World Series.

Age: 29 (in February) 2026 Stats: .231/.312/.399, 19 HR, 55 RBI, 41 SB, 1.7 bWAR Career Stats : .245/.315/.444, 127 HR, 363 RBI, 171 SB, 14.3 bWAR Consensus Contract Projection : 2 years, $22.3M AAV

Jazz Chisholm Jr. picked a most unfortunate time to have his worst season at the plate.

To be sure, he was a far cry from terrible. His strikeout rate was up and his slugging percentage was down, but he still ended up with 19 home runs and basically league-average marks in both wRC+ and OPS+—to go along with great defense and a ton of stolen bases.

All the same, it very much was not the springboard year into lucrative free agency that Chisholm was dreaming about nine months ago, and now he's probably going to need to settle for a "one year plus a player option (or two years' worth of player options)" with plans of trying again next year.

The good news for a team like the Pittsburgh Pirates is now they could make a winning bid on a short-term deal with a guy who was expected to be about $200M out of their price range.

And what a fun short-term deal it could be, replacing Brandon Lowe with Chisholm and pairing him with Oneil Cruz and Konnor Griffin. They could end up racing each other to 50 stolen bases, while Chisholm and Cruz battle for the team lead in home runs.

It's more than the Pirates would normally spend on a top free agent, but their window with Paul Skenes is already rapidly closing. They need to be aggressively trying to win one in the 2027-29 timeframe, or else they might as well just trade Skenes now.

Age: 31 2026 Stats: 185.0 IP, 3.21 ERA, 4.13 FIP, 1.18 WHIP, 7.7 K/9, 4.3 bWAR Career Stats : 679.2 IP, 3.23 ERA, 3.67 FIP, 1.19 WHIP, 9.5 K/9, 15.1 bWAR Consensus Contract Projection : 4 years, $24.7M AAV

Michael King opted out of the final two years on his previous contract, leaving $53M on the table.

However, that doesn't necessarily mean he wants to leave San Diego. He's merely looking to cash in on a longer-term contract for more total money after one of the healthiest and most productive seasons of his career.

Though he did miss about half of the 2025 campaign, he has given the Padres 432.0 innings with a 3.15 ERA since the beginning of 2024. Over the past two seasons, he has made 25 regular season starts at Petco Park with a 2.63 ERA to show for it. He also has given San Diego not one, but two postseason starts in which he went seven scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild card round.

And goodness knows the Padres could use him back.

Of the 14 pitchers who started for San Diego this past season, the only ones still with the franchise are Randy Vásquez and a trio of relievers who each served as openers a few times (Wandy Peralta, Kyle Hart and Bradgley Rodriguez).

Even if we're assuming Joe Musgrove can come back and be their ace after missing two years of action, this rotation still needs a lot of help. And they've already missed out on most of the biggest arms that were available this winter.

Forecasting MLB's Biggest 2027 Bombshells 😲

2026 Stats: .260/.331/.493, 35 HR, 96 RBI, 5.3 bWAR

Career Stats : .250/.327/.483, 192 HR, 542 RBI, 23.1 bWAR

Consensus Contract Projection : 3 years, $22.4M AAV

This past season, Brandon Lowe was one of the most valuable defenders in all of baseball, posting a +15 outs above average . The previous year, however, he posted -14 OAA .

So, who knows what he'll accomplish with his glove on his next contract?

It's the big bat, though, that makes Lowe such a coveted asset.

Since the beginning of 2021, he has clubbed 155 home runs in 2,951 trips to the plate. Those marks are virtually identical to Max Muncy's 156 home runs in 2,978 plate appearances.

Moreover, Lowe's ratio of 19.04 PA/HR is the eighth lowest among players with at least 2,500 PA over the past six seasons, behind only Aaron Judge, Kyle Schwarber, Shohei Ohtani, Cal Raleigh, Pete Alonso, Yordan Alvarez and Matt Olson.

Did you realize he was that great of a slugger? Because I sure didn't.

Meanwhile, the Washington Nationals got a whole lot of nothing on offense from the second base spot last season.

Take out the handful of times CJ Abrams played there and you're left with a group (led mainly by Nasim Nuñez and Jorbit Vivas) that slugged .258.

Just to reiterate, it wasn't a .258 batting average. It was a .258 slugging percentage. We're talking one home run in 499 ABs. And Washington still somehow ranked third in the majors in scoring.

Now imagine if they went instantly from MLB's worst offense at second base to maybe the league's best offense at that position.

If they're not going to sign CJ Abrams or James Wood to long-term extensions, they might as well at least sign Lowe for a few years and try to score 1,000 runs in a season while they still have their stars from the Juan Soto trade.

2026 Stats: 86.0 IP, 2.83 ERA, 2.37 FIP, 1.08 WHIP, 11.2 K/9, 1.9 bWAR

Career Stats : 298.1 IP, 3.26 ERA, 3.04 FIP, 1.18 WHIP, 9.7 K/9, 5.2 bWAR

Consensus Contract Projection : 4 years, $19.1M AAV

While David Bednar accepted his qualifying offer to return to the Yankees for one more year, Adrián Morejón declined his, becoming hands down the most coveted reliever on the market.

That's despite a career high of just three saves.

Since the beginning of 2024, however, Morejón has logged 223.1 innings with a 2.58 ERA—plus another 10.2 innings with a 1.69 ERA in the postseason. There just hasn't been any room in the ninth-inning inn: He spent two years behind Robert Suarez, followed by one behind Mason Miller.

If he wants to be the singular closer for a team with viable World Series aspirations, Morejón's two best options appear to both be in Chicago. We're leaning toward the Cubs as the perfect fit, mostly because they have been more willing to spend big money in the past and because they have the more dire need for another southpaw in their bullpen. Either one could be a great fit, though.

However, don't sleep on the Yankees here.

Since Bednar only took a one-year deal, they could bring in Morejón and play lefty/righty matchups in the eighth and ninth innings for one year. If he holds his own in 2027, they hand the reins to Morejón on a full-time basis once Bednar actually hits free agency next winter.

Age: 32 2026 Stats: .270/.368/.473, 26 HR, 86 RBI, 5.1 bWAR Career Stats : .269/.351/.472, 113 HR, 382 RBI, 16.2 bWAR Consensus Contract Projection : 4 years, $26.2M AAV

As things presently stand, the Toronto Blue Jays have one of the most underwhelming projected starting OF/DH quartets in all of baseball, with FanGraphs forecasting Brett Bateman in center, Nathan Lukes in right, Jonatan Clase in left and Anthony Santander at DH.

Bateman was rock solid as a rookie for the Blue Jays, making his MLB debut less than a week after they got him in the Kevin Gausman trade. And Lukes was, for the second consecutive season, an above-average defender whose left-handed bat was respectable enough against right-handed pitching.

Neither is exactly irreplaceable, though, while Clase and Santander have appeared in a combined total of 97 games since the beginning of last season. (There have also been some rumors of Lukes as a trade candidate.)

Suffice it to say, the Blue Jays are in the market for someone like Randy Arozarena, Ian Happ or Seiya Suzuki.

Why the latter stands out as their preferred target is his metronomic quality production at the plate.

In each of the past four seasons, Suzuki has:

Made enough plate appearances to qualify for a batting title

The only other players who have checked all of those boxes in at least three of the past four seasons are Shohei Ohtani (four), Rafael Devers (four), Juan Soto (three), Freddie Freeman (three), Kyle Schwarber (three) and Yandy Díaz (three).

And if there's one team in baseball that is desperate right now to add a sure thing to its lineup, it's the Toronto Blue Jays, fresh off a disappointing season in which Kazuma Okamoto was probably the only position player who met or exceeded expectations.

They can figure out during spring training whether Suzuki fits better as the primary right fielder or the primary designated hitter, but getting his bat into the lineup would be huge.

articles.title: New MLB Trade Rumors on Eduardo Rodriguez, Merrill Kelly Amid 'Soaring' Pitching Market in FA
articles.summary: The Arizona Diamondbacks have reportedly been receiving calls from teams in need of starting pitching recently.
articles.body:
The Arizona Diamondbacks have reportedly been receiving calls from teams in need of starting pitching recently.

According to Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon of The Athletic, the lofty price of doing business in free agency has prompted teams to inquire about the availability of Eduardo Rodríguez and Merrill Kelly.

That comes in the wake of teams handing out massive contracts to starting pitchers in recent days, including the Chicago Cubs signing Trevor Rogers to a five-year, $120 million deal, and the Baltimore Orioles inking Freddy Peralta to a five-year, $125 million pact.

Forecasting MLB's Biggest 2027 Bombshells 😲

Both Rodríguez and Kelly are playing under more palatable contracts, as Rodríguez is signed for two more years at $20 million per season, while Kelly will make $20 million next season before becoming a free agent.

Rodríguez, a 33-year-old southpaw from Venezuela, is surprisingly coming off the best season of his career.

After posting an ERA over 5.00 in both 2024 and 2025, Rodríguez posted a 16-7 record with a career-low 2.89 ERA, plus a 1.24 WHIP and 143 strikeouts over 189.2 innings.

A 2018 World Series champion with the Boston Red Sox, Rodríguez was named an All-Star for the first time in his career last season, and he had success by focusing less on piling up strikeouts, as his K rate of 6.8 per nine innings was a career low and paled in comparison to his career strikeout rate of 8.7.

Kelly is a 38-year-old righty who experienced far more ups and downs than Rodríguez did last season.

He went 10-14 with a career-worst 4.94 ERA and 1.46 WHIP, while striking out 113 batters over 162 innings pitched.

Kelly entered 2026 having posted an ERA of 4.03 or better and a WHIP of 1.19 or better in four consecutive seasons. He also never averaged less than 7.4 strikeouts per nine innings in a season before averaging just 6.3 last season.

By almost all measures, last season was the worst of Kelly's career, but he has been a highly consistent performer over the years, and he doesn't carry a ton of risk since there is only one year remaining on his contract.

Of course, it isn't entirely clear how willing the D-backs would be to move one or both of Rodríguez and Kelly.

Since their shocking run to the World Series in 2023, the Diamondbacks have missed the playoffs in three straight seasons. They did post a record over .500 in two of those years, though, including last season when they went 86-76.

That suggests Arizona may be more apt to add than subtract, but if the offers are good enough, perhaps the Diamondbacks could be convinced to move on from at least one of their veteran starters.

articles.title: New MLB Rumors on Orioles' Free Agency, Trade Targets After Freddy Peralta Contract
articles.summary: After giving Freddy Peralta the richest contract for a pitcher in franchise history, the Baltimore Orioles may not be done making moves to improve for 2027.
articles.body:
After giving Freddy Peralta the richest contract for a pitcher in franchise history, the Baltimore Orioles may not be done making moves to improve for 2027.

Per The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon , the Orioles could use their "depth of infielders and upper-level pitching prospects" as they look at potential trades for starting pitchers.

The report also notes Baltimore wants to add an outfielder in free agency, with Ian Happ, Mauricio Dubón and Myles Straw cited as players the club has expressed an interest.

Peralta, who agreed to a five-year, $125 million deal on Tuesday, is essentially taking Trevor Rogers' spot in the rotation after Rogers agreed to a five-year, $120 million contract with the Chicago Cubs.

The one-for-one move does provide the Orioles some stability at the top of their rotation. Peralta could end up being an upgrade over Rogers because he has a longer track record of health and is just one year removed from a fifth-place finish in NL Cy Young voting.

Since the Orioles have shown some willingness to spend aggressively in free agency — Peralta's deal comes after they signed Pete Alonso in free agency last year — their best approach would be to keep going as they look to compete in the AL East.

Right field, in particular, is a position the Orioles need help. They got a collective .219/.294/.348 slash line and had the seventh-worst wRC+ from the position in 2026.

Happ is the most accomplished of the three potential Baltimore targets with four Gold Glove awards and an All-Star appearance in 2022 on his resume. Dubón is coming off his best offensive season with a .276 batting average and 12 homers in 153 games for Atlanta.

Straw's value is primarily on defense because he hasn't had a wRC+ higher than 91 since 2021. He could step in to play center for the Orioles if they were to trade Colton Cowser in an effort to add more pitching help.

articles.title: New Mets Rumors on Roster Priorities After Historic Tarik Skubal Contract in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Having made their big splash of the offseason with Tarik Skubal's historic nine-year, $450 million contract, the New York Mets will now turn their attention to filling out their roster for the 2027 season.
articles.body:
Having made their big splash of the offseason with Tarik Skubal's historic nine-year, $450 million contract, the New York Mets will now turn their attention to filling out their roster for the 2027 season.

Per The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon , the Mets are looking at right-handed hitting bench outfielders to join their starting group of Juan Soto, Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing.

The Mets already solved their platoon issue at first base by signing Paul Goldschmidt to split reps with Jared Young.

Nick Morabito, a second-round pick in the 2022 draft, is currently penciled in as New York's fourth outfielder. He made his MLB debut last season, appearing in 19 games across two stints and posting a .195/.283/.244 slash line.

Among the remaining free agents who could potentially fill the role of a fourth outfielder are Adolis García, Lane Thomas and Myles Straw.

Thomas and Straw are both capable of playing center field when they are called upon. García has played center in the past, but his time there has been limited to a total of eight innings over the past three seasons combined.

None of them would dramatically alter the race in the NL East for 2027, but the Mets found out the hard way last season what life without a solid fourth outfielder looks like.

Soto missed 51 games due to calf injuries, leading to a lot of plate appearances for players like Morabito, Tyrone Taylor and MJ Melendez.

The Mets outfield looks stacked as presently constructed. Soto is a superstar at the plate. Benge is coming off a breakout rookie year. Ewing is a strong defender in center who hits well enough to be a quality starter.

As long as that group is healthy next season, the Mets should be a much bigger factor in the NL playoff race than they were in 2026 when it felt like everything that could go wrong for them did en route to a 74-88 record.

articles.title: Top MLB Trade Rumors Ahead of 2026 Winter Meetings
articles.summary: The 2026 MLB offseason is shifting into warp speed.
articles.body:
The 2026 MLB offseason is shifting into warp speed.

While the Winter Meetings often kick things into high gear, the possible impending lockout—which could morph the meetings into discussing minor-league business only—is responsible for this recent flurry of activity.

With the clock steadily ticking toward the expiration of the current collective bargaining agreement, fans should expect to see this recent run of deals continue—if not accelerate. As for what could be coming next, let's hit the latest rumor-mill rumblings to find out.

Corey Seager Has Fondness for Philadelphia?

With shortstop Corey Seager struggling to stay on the field, and the Texas Rangers struggling to escape mediocrity's grasp, a fresh start might be best for everyone involved. But the fact that the five-time All-Star has no-trade protection limits the possible outcomes a bit.

That said, Seager is reportedly willing to waive that no-trade clause to join the Philadelphia Phillies, per NBC Sports Philadelphia .

A healthy Seager—or even a healthy-ish Seager—can still be a difference-maker. When he plays, he produces. He missed exactly 60 games each of the past two seasons and still found his way to 41 homers, 118 runs and 101 RBI over this stretch.

Adding Seager, a positive defender, might bump incumbent Trea Turner to the outfield, and it would deepen a lineup that needs more mashers alongside Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper. The interest, in other words, could absolutely be mutual.

Giants Setting High Asking Price for Logan Webb?

The San Francisco Giants have a pricey payroll and a roster that isn't performing (97 losses with a minus-91 run differential). That's a combo that almost always leads to significant changes, and this situation sounds no different.

The Giants are "open to listening to offers" for ace pitcher and three-time All-Star Logan Webb, per FanSided's Robert Murray . They also seemingly want to be blown away by an offer, and there's a chance that kind of interest just doesn't exist.

"San Francisco would want a 'very strong return' for Webb, according to a person briefed on the team's plans who was not authorized to discuss trade conversations publicly," Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon reported for The Athletic. "And while a number of clubs are desperate to add starting pitching, some rival executives are skeptical the Giants will get their price."

Webb has never been a big strikeout pitcher, but he has typically tallied a bunch of innings while keeping runs off the board. That said, he didn't live up to his standard in either department this past season, when he posted a 4.31 ERA (his worst since 2020) across 160.2 innings (200-plus the previous three years).

Now, maybe the demand for pitching helps offset some of this statistical decline, but the Giants probably aren't fetching a haul here. So, unless they are realistic about what they can bring back, maybe these talks about Webb will yield nothing more than conversations.

The Arizona Diamondbacks need pitching help. They might have an idea of how to find it, too.

Per USA Today 's Bob Nightengale , the Diamondbacks "need to clear payroll by moving former All-Star second baseman Ketel Marte" to free up the funds needed to pursue free agent pitchers. Nightengale added that Arizona "would love to trade him before the lockout" and could "if the Blue Jays or Tampa Bay Rays get serious."

Marte, Nightengale noted, has a no-trade clause, so Arizona could need his assistance in getting something done. And it's hard to say what kind of market he'll have if front offices think his star might be fading. Despite playing his most games in three years in 2026, his offensive production was his worst of this stretch (22 homers, 78 runs scored and a .249/.316/.432 slash line).

That said, he's a three-time All-Star, and his age (33) isn't necessarily setting off huge decline-related alarms. He should be able to find a new baseball home if he wants one, although Arizona's apparent eagerness to get something done won't help the potential return.
