articles.title: Alec Bohm Reportedly Lands Royals Contract in MLB FA amid Yankees, Mets Rumors
articles.summary: Veteran third baseman Alec Bohm is on the move after agreeing to a deal with the Kansas City Royals.
articles.body:
Veteran third baseman Alec Bohm is on the move after agreeing to a deal with the Kansas City Royals.

Per MLB Network's Jon Morosi , Bohm and the Royals reached an agreement in free agency on Wednesday.

Forecasting MLB's Biggest 2027 Bombshells 😲

Bohm was rumored to be targeted by both the New York Mets and New York Yankees this offseason, but he chose to take his talents to the Midwest.

Bohm has spent his entire career with the Philadelphia Phillies up until this point. He was originally selected with the No. 3 pick in the 2018 draft, then made his MLB debut two years later.

The 30-year-old had an up-and-down seven-year run with the Phillies. His peak came in 2024 when he was named to the NL All-Star team.

Bohm's best stretch in his career thus far came from 2023 to '25. He was an above-average hitter by wRC+ in each of those three seasons, posting a .280/.330/.433 slash line in 408 games.

Last season was a step back at the plate. Bohm hit .249/.315/.383 with 15 homers in 155 games for a 90 wRC+ and .277 wOBA that ranked last among 17 third baseman with at least 400 plate appearances.

One encouraging sign from 2026 came late in the season when Bohm hit .305/.383/.424 in 201 plate appearances over 50 games from Aug. 1 through Sept. 27. This at least suggests Bohm figured some things out, so his upside going forward could be higher than his overall numbers suggest.

There are also other underlying metrics that suggest Bohm wasn't as bad as his overall 2026 slash line. He ranked in the 87th percentile or better in whiff rate, strikeout rate and squared-up rate.

If Bohm can make more consistently hard contact, there is upside for him to get back to being at least a league-average hitter in 2027. His defense is still good as he finished in the 89th percentile with five outs above average playing primarily at the hot corner.

Bohm is joining a Royals team that went 69-93 in 2026 and missed the playoffs for the second straight year.

articles.title: Royce Lewis Says He Asked for Matt Kemp's Permission to Wear No. 27 Jersey with Dodgers
articles.summary: After being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers last week, Royce Lewis has revealed he will wear No. 27 for his new team.
articles.body:
After being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers last week, Royce Lewis has revealed he will wear No. 27 for his new team.

Appearing on AM 570 LA Sports' Dodger Talk show, Lewis explained he received Matt Kemp's blessing to use his former Dodgers number.

Lewis wore No. 23 throughout his entire tenure with the Minnesota Twins. Catcher Ryan Jeffers switched from No. 39 to 27 in 2021, the season before Lewis made his MLB debut.

The Dodgers acquired Lewis from the Minnesota Twins for Bobby Miller and Francisco Espinoza. It's something of a challenge trade for Lewis and Miller, both former first-round picks who have not yet lived up to their initial potential.

Lewis may not open the 2027 season as a starter in Los Angeles because its a crowded roster, but his versatility with experience at all four infield spots and some history in both corner outfield positions could lead to him getting plenty of playing time.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2017 draft, Lewis' pro career has largely been defined by injuries to this point. His career-high in games played is 126, set last season.

Lewis has surpassed the 100-game barrier in each of the last two years, but his offensive output has declined with more playing time. His best season came in 2023 when he hit .309/.372/.548 with 15 homers in 239 plate appearances across 58 games.

Kemp spent 10 of his 15 MLB seasons with the Dodgers. He wore No. 27 in 14 of 15 years, switching to 25 for his final year with the Colorado Rockies in 2020 because Trevor Story had 27.

During his tenure with the Dodgers, Kemp made two All-Star appearances, won two Gold Glove awards and two Silver Slugger awards. He finished second in NL MVP voting in 2011.

After his playing career ended, Kemp returned to the Dodgers organization in 2024 in an advisory role.

articles.title: Major League Baseball Sues Players' Union, Asking Court to Declare Lockout is Legal
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Signaling the likely start next week of a long and acrimonious lockout, Major League Baseball sued its players' association in federal court on Wednesday, trying to head off any attempt by the union to decertify and challenge the work stoppage with an antitrust case.
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Signaling the likely start next week of a long and acrimonious lockout, Major League Baseball sued its players' association in federal court on Wednesday, trying to head off any attempt by the union to decertify and challenge the work stoppage with an antitrust case.

In a 38-page complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, MLB and the corporate entities owning its 30 teams sued the Major League Baseball Players Association and the eight players on the union's executive subcommittee, including pitcher Tarik Skubal just days after he agreed to a record $450 million contract with the New York Mets.

"MLB brings this action to keep the dispute over the next collective bargaining agreement at the bargaining table, where federal law says it belongs," the lawsuit said. "MLB has a reasonable and imminent fear that the union will attempt to use the threat of antitrust liability to derail the collective bargaining process altogether in favor of antitrust litigation."

Owners have proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994, when players fought off the proposal with a 7 1/2-month strike that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years.

Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred said last week he can't imagine owners approving an agreement without a cap and players have vowed never to accept one, leaving the sport headed to its 10th work stoppage since 1972.

"MLB expects to exercise its right to implement a lockout upon expiration of the CBA at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, 2026, in support of its lawful bargaining position," the lawsuit said.

MLB said in the suit it intends to file an unfair labor practice charge with the National Labor Relations Board, alleging the union has refused to bargain in good faith.

"The long-term health of professional baseball depends on competitive balance, on keeping smaller-market clubs viable, and on better pay for all players, not just a handful of superstars," the suit said.

The U.S. Supreme Court in its 1996 decision in Brown v. Pro Football Inc. ruled unionized employees may not file antitrust suits and must rely on labor law — what has become known as the nonstatutory labor exemption. As a result, union leaderships in the past have filed disclaimers of interest that they no longer wish to represent the bargaining unit and union members have filed decertification petitions.

"The lawyers and officials leading the union have no real intention of abandoning their role leading the players' negotiating efforts," the suit said. "Instead, those lawyers and officials will use the threat of antitrust injunctions and treble damages to try to coerce MLB into caving to their bargaining demands. If they succeed in their gambit, they will then spontaneously resurrect the MLBPA and enter into a new CBA."

Owners asked for a declaratory judgment determining a lockout doesn't violate antitrust laws and doesn't amount to an unreasonable restraint of trade. They asked for a ruling that the federal courts lack jurisdiction to enjoin a lockout and for an order that the players be defined as a legal class, which if granted could block individual lawsuits.

"The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous," the union said in a statement. "We will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing."

Among the lawyers representing MLB are Paul D. Clement, Solicitor General in the President George W. Bush administration, and Keker, Van Nest & Peters, which represented the union in litigation from 2003-09 against federal government seizure of player drug tests.

Players' outside counsel includes Jeffrey Kessler, a former law partner of Bruce Meyer, who took over as union head in February. MLB anticipates the possibility of antitrust ligation because Kessler and/or Meyer worked for players' unions at a time when decertification or disclaimer attempts took place by players in the NFL (1989), NBA (1987, 1995 and 2011) and NHL (2012).

"Today's filing is a defensive measure simply intended to keep the parties at the bargaining table to work towards a new collective bargaining agreement and a full 2027 season," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "We believe the union is preparing to follow the playbook its new leadership has used against other major professional sports leagues by pretending to 'disclaim' its status as the players' bargaining process."

Caplin referred decertification as a "nuclear option," mirroring Meyer's description of the salary cap proposal as a "nuclear bomb."

"Despite the many efforts by MLB to find common ground with the MLBPA, the union has categorically refused to engage with MLB's salary cap and floor structure," the suit stated. "The union has not engaged in good-faith bargaining over the central economic issues in these negotiations, even as the expiration of the current CBA is imminent."

articles.title: MLB sues MLBPA days before possible lockout; union calls lawsuit 'incredibly disappointing'
articles.summary: The MLBPA could dissolve itself as a negotiating tactic.
articles.body:
MLB is launching a preemptive strike against the union ahead of a possible lockout. Days before the expiration of the current collective bargaining agreement, the league sued the MLBPA in an attempt to keep the league's antitrust exemption, per multiple reports.

With the lawsuit, the league is hoping the courts rule that the players cannot dissolve their union , per Evan Drellich of The Athletic.

While it seems counterintuitive for the players to dissolve the union ahead of — or during — a lockout, there's a strategic reason the players might make that move. If the MLBPA decides to dissolve, it would open MLB to more lawsuits challenging its antitrust status.

With a union in place, labor law — not antitrust law — takes precedence. If the MLBPA dissolves, however, that would open a path for the players to sue the league and challenge its antitrust exemption.

There has already been chatter that the league might face legal challenges to its antitrust exemption. In November, Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) introduced a bill that would reexamine whether MLB should retain its antitrust exemption. Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) co-sponsored the bill.

The league has faced antitrust challenges over the years, though it has retained that status. Other sports leagues, such as the NFL, do not benefit from that same exemption.

When news of Durbin's and Lee's bill came to light , the MLBPA said it was "gratified," per The Athletic. The union called the league's exemption "judicially created and unique," in a statement.

In response to Wednesday's lawsuit, MLBPA called the move "incredibly disappointing" in a statement, per Drellich.

"The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous. We will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing."

The league claimed the lawsuit was a "defensive measure" aimed to " keep the parties at the bargaining table ," in a statement.

The developments come just days before the league's current CBA is set to expire. If both sides can't agree on a new CBA prior to Dec. 1 — which is unlikely, considering the state of negotiations in late November — the league would lock out the players .

The MLBPA has not indicated a desire to dissolve publicly, though it's a tactic the union could take, depending on how contentious or drawn out negotiations become. MLB's lawsuit seeks to prevent that option, though it also creates more animosity between the two sides at a time when tensions and emotions are already high.

articles.title: Jonathan Loaisiga's Decision to Turn Down Mets for Yankees Revealed in New MLB Rumors
articles.summary: The New York Mets offered "slightly more money" to right-handed relief pitcher Jonathan Loáisiga than the New York Yankees did in free agency, but the 32-year-old ultimately decided to return to the Bronx, where he pitched from 2018-2025 before heading to the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2026, per Jon Heyman of the New York Post.
articles.body:
The New York Mets offered "slightly more money" to right-handed relief pitcher Jonathan Loáisiga than the New York Yankees did in free agency, but the 32-year-old ultimately decided to return to the Bronx, where he pitched from 2018-2025 before heading to the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2026, per Jon Heyman of the New York Post .

Loáisiga agreed to a two-year deal worth $19 million guaranteed ($9.5 million in 2027 and 2028), per ESPN's Jorge Castillo . The Yankees hold a $9.5 million club option for 2029 and will pay a $500,000 buyout should they decline it.

Loáisiga also got a $500,000 signing bonus and will receive up to $750,000 in performance bonuses in both 2027 and 2028.

The righty posted a 2.42 ERA (1.03 WHIP) in 67 games (67 innings) for the D-backs. He struck out 48 batters and walked just 13.

It was an impressive comeback for Loáisiga, who has made just 50 appearances ove the last three seasons due to injury. Of note, he underwent surgery to remove a bone spur in 2023 and suffered a torn UCL in 2024 and a flexor strain in 2025 .

However, Loáisiga showed great form in 2026, and now he's back with the Yankees, who have made some bullpen moves by signing left-handed reliever Brent Suter and re-signing left-handed relief pitcher Tim Hill this offseason.

articles.title: Latest Yankees Rumors Reveal New Reliever Target in MLB Free Agency Amid Adrian Morejon Buzz
articles.summary: Adrian Morejon is not the only reliever the New York Yankees are reportedly targeting this offseason.
articles.body:
Adrian Morejon is not the only reliever the New York Yankees are reportedly targeting this offseason.

The Yankees "have shown interest" in free agent left-hander Alex Vesia, according to The Athletic's Brendan Kuty and Will Sammon .

Kuty and Sammon noted "about a half-dozen teams are showing serious interest in Vesia."

Vesia recorded a 2.64 ERA across 72 appearances and 58 innings pitched in 2026 during his sixth season with the Los Angeles Dodgers.

ESPN's Jeff Passan previously reported Vesia is looking for three years on his next contract "and could get it."

Sportsnet's Ben Nicholson-Smith and Shi Davidi previously reported the Toronto Blue Jays had interest in Vesia.

The Athletic's Katie Woo also reported the New York Mets and Miami Marlins "have expressed serious interest," while USA Today's Bob Nightengale reported the Arizona Diamondbacks have Vesia "on their radar."

The Yankees could still look to pursue Vesia, especially if the club falls short in its pursuit of Morejon, who The Athletic's Mitch Bannon reported is also "engaged" with the Toronto Blue Jays.

Kuty previously reported that as of Tuesday night, the Yankees "were still among the teams in the hunt" for Morejon, who is hitting free agency after recording a 2.83 ERA across 76 appearances and 86.0 innings pitched last season with the San Diego Padres.

The Yankees' pursuit of Vesia and Morejon follows general manager Brian Cashman following up on his statement that adding to the bullpen was his "main priority" this offseason.

David Bednar has also accepted a $23.15 million qualifying offer to rejoin the Yankees, which also brought back Tim Hill and signed free agent Brent Suter on one-year contracts .

Jonathan Loáisiga is also returning to the Yankees after one season with the Arizona Diamondbacks on a two-year, $19 million guaranteed deal with a $9.5 million club option for 2029, per ESPN's Jorge Castillo .

Kuty previously noted that adding more relievers would help the Yankees bolster their bullpen depth while giving the club "flexibility to consider trading from their deep stash of starting pitching."

What pitchers Cashman is able to consider placing on the trade block in the future could hinge on whether he is able to bring in Vesia or Morejon before the current CBA expires next Tuesday.
